first.where: Perceptual organization and the judgment of brightness. Science 262(5142): 2042–2044

entries.effectEn: Identical grey patches on a folded plaid surface look strikingly different depending on whether they read as lying on an illuminated or a shaded face.

mechanismEn.name: Perceived 3D layout determines which patches are grouped into the same illumination framework

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9.

impl.notes: Share the WebGL scene with checker-shadow: one folded surface, orbitable camera, movable light. Flattening the fold with a slider kills the effect and makes the depth dependence visible.

first.by: Josef Zihl, Detlev von Cramon and N. Mai
first.where: Selective disturbance of movement vision after bilateral brain damage. Brain 106(2): 313–340

entries.effectEn: Motion stops being visible. The world arrives as a series of stills: coffee appears frozen in mid-pour, and a person crossing the room is first here and then there.

mechanismEn.name: Bilateral damage to area V5/MT, which removes motion perception while leaving form and colour intact — the strongest single piece of evidence that motion is computed separately

entries.notesEn: The case that proved the visual system has a dedicated motion module. Extraordinarily rare — a handful of documented cases.

impl.notes: The inverse of every motion illusion in the catalogue and a good closing exhibit for that section: a scene the visitor can switch from continuous to strobed stills, with the patient account alongside. Frame it as what it is like to lose something, not as a trick.

first.where: Commentary on Aristotle Meteorologica, c. 200 CE

entries.effectEn: The sky between the primary and secondary rainbow is visibly darker than the sky outside either.

mechanismEn.name: No light is scattered back into that angular band by either one or two internal reflections, so it receives less light than anywhere else

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: The syndrome of Alice in Wonderland. Canadian Medical Association Journal 73(9): 701–704

entries.effectEn: Objects, or parts of ones own body, appear drastically larger (macropsia) or smaller (micropsia) than they are; distance and time can distort with them.

mechanismEn.name: Transient dysfunction in parietal and occipital cortex, most often with migraine, epilepsy or Epstein-Barr infection
mechanismEn.by: Todd 1955 and the later clinical literature

entries.notesEn: Included because the clinical literature describes illusions the perception textbooks never list, and they are the same phenomena approached from the other side.

impl.notes: Not reproducible and not a demonstration. An explanatory page with patient drawings and the Carroll connection. Written as a condition, not a curiosity.

first.where: Drawing, 1892; widely reproduced from 1902

entries.effectEn: A woman seated at a mirrored dressing table, which at a distance is a human skull.

mechanismEn.name: A hybrid-image-like dependence on spatial frequency combined with figure-ground reorganisation

entries.notesEn: Catalogue note: the automated Wikipedia pass matched this title to a 2017 music album. Left in the log as a reminder that mechanical harvesting needs a human pass.

impl.notes: Public domain. A zoom-out or blur slider makes the skull emerge, which is the correct way to present it.

first.by: Douglas R. Hofstadter coined the term; the form is much older
first.where: Hofstadter, Metamagical Themas, Basic Books, 1985 (term coined 1983–84)

entries.effectEn: A word that reads as the same word, or a different one, when rotated or reflected.

mechanismEn.name: Letter identification tolerates large deformation, so one glyph can satisfy two letter hypotheses at two orientations

entries.notesEn: A Cyrillic ambigram set would be genuinely unusual and fits the trilingual site.

impl.notes: A rotation control over our own drawn ambigrams. A generator is a much bigger project and probably not worth it; a small hand-made set in three alphabets, including Cyrillic, is more distinctive.

first.by: The rabbit-duck in Fliegende Blätter is the earliest widely cited instance
first.where: Fliegende Blätter, 23 October 1892

entries.effectEn: One picture, two or more incompatible readings.

mechanismEn.name: Object hypotheses competing over shared evidence

impl.notes: Umbrella gallery, all public-domain: rabbit-duck, Hill wife/mother-in-law, Gilbert All Is Vanity, Arcimboldo, plus our own commissioned or generated one.

first.where: Patented 1940; published and made reproducible by Ittelson, The Ames Demonstrations in Perception, Princeton University Press, 1952

entries.effectEn: Two people of equal height standing in opposite corners of a trapezoidal room look like a giant and a child, from the one viewpoint the room was built for.

mechanismEn.name: The assumption that the room is rectangular is stronger than the evidence about the people, so the people are rescaled instead of the room

entries.notesEn: The Honi phenomenon: observers see less distortion when the person in the room is their own spouse. Replications are mixed, so treat it as a story rather than a finding.

impl.notes: The best possible WebGL exhibit in the catalogue: build the real trapezoidal geometry, lock the camera to the viewing hole, then let the visitor unlock it and orbit. The moment the room reveals itself as a wedge is the payoff, and it is impossible in a photograph.

first.where: Visual perception and the rotating trapezoidal window. Psychological Monographs: General and Applied 65(7): 1–32

entries.effectEn: A trapezoidal window rotating steadily in one direction is seen swinging back and forth instead — and a rod pushed through it appears to pass through solid frame.

mechanismEn.name: The trapezoid is interpreted as a rectangular window seen in perspective, so its longer edge is always taken as the nearer one, which forces an oscillation

entries.notesEn: Cross-cultural work in the 1960s claimed people from non-rectangular architectural environments are less susceptible. The evidence is thin and the site should say so.

impl.notes: WebGL window on a constant-speed rotation, with a rod that can be attached and a slider that morphs the trapezoid back into a rectangle. At rectangle the illusion dies — that sweep is the argument.

first.by: Leonardo da Vinci (earliest known example); the term coined by Gaspar Schott, 1657
first.where: Leonardo, Codex Atlanticus, c. 1485 (the anamorphic eye); Holbein, The Ambassadors, 1533; Schott, Magia universalis naturae et artis, 1657

entries.effectEn: A distorted image resolves into a recognisable one from a single oblique viewpoint, or when reflected in a cylindrical mirror.

mechanismEn.name: The projection is constructed to be correct from one station point; from anywhere else it is a smear

entries.notesEn: Holbein skull in The Ambassadors (1533) is the most famous instance and is out of copyright.

impl.notes: Two modes: an oblique anamorphosis the visitor rotates the camera around until it snaps into place, and a catoptric one with a virtual cylindrical mirror. The mathematics is a straightforward inverse projection, so this is mostly a presentation problem.

first.where: Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185(4157): 1124–1131

entries.effectEn: A number you have just seen — even a demonstrably random one — shifts your next numeric estimate toward it.

mechanismEn.name: Estimation starts from an available value and adjusts insufficiently

entries.notesEn: Among the more robust findings in the field, though effect sizes in replications are smaller than the originals.

impl.notes: Randomly assign each visitor a high or low anchor, ask an estimation question, and show the two distributions afterwards. A genuine between-subjects experiment on a web page, and the visitor sees their own group mean. Needs the assignment to be honest and the debrief to be immediate.

first.where: Problemata; also referred to in Metaphysics IV

entries.effectEn: Cross your index and middle fingers and roll a small bead between the tips. You feel two beads.

mechanismEn.name: The two contacted surfaces are on opposite sides of the fingers, which in the normal uncrossed posture could only be touched by two separate objects

entries.notesEn: Two and a half thousand years old and still works on everyone, which is a point worth making about the stability of these phenomena.

impl.notes: The one entry in this batch every visitor can do immediately with no equipment — a pea, a bead, the tip of their own nose. Instructions and a diagram are the whole exhibit. Put it first in the tactile section for exactly that reason.

first.by: The underlying glare effect is Zavagno 1999; the petal figure is Kitaoka
first.where: Zavagno, Some new luminance-gradient effects. Perception 28(7): 835–838, 1999; the Asahi arrangement is published on Kitaoka illusion pages

entries.effectEn: A flower of petals shading from dark at the tips to light at the centre makes the white centre look self-luminous, brighter than the page it is printed on.

mechanismEn.name: Luminance gradients converging on a region are read as a glare source, and perceived brightness exceeds the physical maximum

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9 by separating the effect (Zavagno 1999) from the figure (Kitaoka). Still the best opening exhibit in the brightness section.

impl.notes: Procedural petals with sliders on gradient steepness and petal count; a control with the gradient reversed shows the effect is directional.

first.by: Jane E. Raymond, Kimron L. Shapiro and Karen M. Arnell
first.where: Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: an attentional blink? JEP:HPP 18(3): 849–860

entries.effectEn: Spot one target in a rapid stream of letters and you become briefly blind to a second target arriving 200 to 500 ms later.

mechanismEn.name: Attentional resources are still committed to consolidating the first target when the second arrives

entries.notesEn: One of the clearest cases where a visitor can generate a textbook curve from their own responses on a web page.

impl.notes: An RSVP stream at about 10 items per second with two targets at varying lag. Plotting the visitor accuracy against lag reproduces the classic U-shaped curve in about three minutes of trials. Frame timing must be measured, not assumed.

first.where: Reported in Kosmos 3: 73–74; Humboldt thought the motion of the stars was real

entries.effectEn: A single stationary point of light in total darkness wanders unpredictably.

mechanismEn.name: With no reference frame, small eye movements and drift in the oculomotor signal cannot be distinguished from real motion of the target

entries.notesEn: Behind a large share of historical UFO reports, and behind Sherif classic demonstration that group consensus can form around a stimulus with no true answer.

impl.notes: Needs a genuinely dark room and a full-screen black page with one dim dot. Add the Sherif twist: ask the visitor how far it moved, then show the distribution of everyone else answers. The convergence is the interesting part.

first.by: Christopher W. Tyler, with Maureen B. Clarke
first.where: First single-image random-dot stereogram produced 1979; published as The autostereogram, Proc. SPIE 1256: 182–197, 1990

entries.effectEn: A flat field of repeating texture resolves into a three-dimensional scene when the eyes are diverged or converged away from the page.

mechanismEn.name: Horizontal repetition periods encode disparity; the visual system matches the wrong repetition and computes depth from the mismatch

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/depth-3d. Roughly one person in ten cannot fuse them at all — which also makes it a member of the proposed population-split class.

impl.notes: Generate from our own depth maps in a worker — the algorithm is short and the result is unmistakably ours. Add a depth-map upload and a wall-eyed/cross-eyed toggle, and a guide-dot pair, because a large share of visitors never free-fuse without one.

first.where: Illusory movement from a rotating barber pole. The American Journal of Psychology 41(4): 686–687

entries.effectEn: Stripes on a rotating cylinder move horizontally, but are seen travelling vertically, along the pole.

mechanismEn.name: The aperture problem: a moving edge seen through a limited window is ambiguous, and the visual system resolves it using the terminators at the window borders

entries.notesEn: The best single entry point to the aperture problem, which underlies most of the rest of this category.

impl.notes: Grating behind a rectangular aperture whose aspect ratio is a slider. Rotating the aperture 90 degrees flips the perceived direction while the physical motion is unchanged — that is the whole argument in one control.

first.where: Beobachtungen zu einem Experiment über Helligkeitskontrast. Psychologische Forschung 5: 131–142

entries.effectEn: Two identical grey triangles on a black cross look different in lightness although their immediate surroundings are identical.

mechanismEn.name: Belongingness: one triangle is seen as part of the cross, the other as part of the background
Coarse spatial sampling reproduces the effect without grouping

entries.notesEn: The clean case for belongingness, because local surround is controlled by construction.

impl.notes: Toggle that lifts the triangles off the cross and places them on a plain field; the difference collapses.

first.by: Bénédict Prévost (first observation); Gustav Fechner (1838); Charles E. Benham (1894, the top)
first.where: Benham, The artificial spectrum top. Nature 51(1308): 200, 1894

entries.effectEn: A spinning disc marked only in black and white produces distinct bands of colour.

mechanismEn.name: The three cone-driven pathways have different temporal responses, so a black-and-white flicker pattern drives them out of balance and the result is read as hue

entries.notesEn: The colours differ between observers and reverse with spin direction, which is worth surfacing: it is one of the clearest cases of an illusion that is not the same for everyone.

impl.notes: Canvas disc with a speed slider. Frame rate matters enormously here — the effect depends on flicker timing, so the implementation must drive rotation from requestAnimationFrame timestamps rather than a fixed step, and should warn that results vary by display refresh rate.

first.where: Experimentelle Studien über das Sehen von Bewegung. Zeitschrift für Psychologie 61: 161–265

entries.effectEn: Two shapes flashed in sequence at nearby positions are seen as one shape moving between them.

mechanismEn.name: The correspondence problem solved in favour of one object in motion rather than two objects appearing and vanishing

entries.notesEn: This, not persistence of vision and not phi, is what makes film work. The persistence-of-vision story has been discredited since Anderson and Anderson (1978) and is still in most textbooks.

impl.notes: Presented inside the phi exhibit as one regime of the same control.

first.where: Die Farbenlehre im Hinblick auf Kunst und Kunstgewerbe. Westermann, Braunschweig, 1874

entries.effectEn: One colour looks different depending on whether it is interlaced with black or white lines — and it shifts toward them, not away, which is the opposite of contrast.

mechanismEn.name: Assimilation: at fine spatial scales the visual system averages rather than contrasts

entries.notesEn: Same identifier as colour-assimilation in the worklist; merged here, with colour-assimilation kept as an alias.

impl.notes: One base colour, a line-width slider that sweeps from thick (contrast) to thin (assimilation). Crossing the point where the effect reverses is the demonstration.

first.where: Repertorium der Physik, 1839

entries.effectEn: Two tones a few hertz apart, one to each ear, produce a slow throbbing beat that exists in neither ear.

mechanismEn.name: The beat is generated centrally, in the binaural comparison, not acoustically — unlike ordinary beats, which are in the air

entries.notesEn: The claims that binaural beats entrain brainwaves, improve focus or induce meditative states are not supported by good evidence, and the site should say so plainly. The perceptual phenomenon is real and interesting on its own.

impl.notes: Two oscillators, one per channel, with a difference-frequency slider. Trivial to build. The page must distinguish binaural beats (central, needs headphones) from ordinary acoustic beats (in the air, works on speakers) — a toggle between the two makes the difference audible in one click.

first.where: De refractione optices parte libri novem. Salviani, Naples, 1593

entries.effectEn: Show each eye a different image and you do not see a blend — you see one, then the other, alternating indefinitely.

mechanismEn.name: Competition between monocular representations, resolved dynamically; heavily used to separate what is on the retina from what is consciously seen

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/ambiguous into the new binocular category, which the audit confirmed against Howard and Rogers and against section VIII of the Oxford Compendium. Rivalry is still ambiguity, and the Gregory axis records that separately from the category.

impl.notes: Needs free-fusing or an anaglyph; both are viable in a browser. Include a printable cardboard-divider template, which is the reliable method. Hold-to-report again, shared with the multistable exhibit.

first.where: Visual perception of biological motion and a model for its analysis. Perception & Psychophysics 14(2): 201–211

entries.effectEn: A dozen moving dots attached to the joints of an otherwise invisible person are instantly and unmistakably a walking human — and observers can read sex, mood and intention from them.

mechanismEn.name: A dedicated system for the kinematics of animate motion, with a locus in superior temporal sulcus

entries.notesEn: The scrambled control is the striking part: identical local motions, no percept at all.

impl.notes: Motion-capture data driving twelve dots. We would need to record our own walk cycle or use an openly licensed dataset — this is the one entry in the batch with a real data-sourcing question. Add a scramble control: randomise the dot start positions and the walker disappears completely while every dot keeps its exact trajectory.

first.where: Nouvelle découverte touchant la veue. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1668

entries.effectEn: Each eye has a hole in its retina where the optic nerve leaves, and you never see the hole — the visual system paints over it with whatever surrounds it.

mechanismEn.name: Active filling-in: the region is completed with surrounding texture and colour rather than merely ignored

entries.notesEn: Mariotte 1668 is the oldest citation in this catalogue that is still a live demonstration anyone can repeat in thirty seconds.

impl.notes: Classic dot-and-cross calibration first, then the interesting part: put the blind spot over a gap in a line and watch the line complete itself, and over a patch of texture and watch the texture continue. Needs an on-screen ruler and a stated viewing distance to work reliably.

first.by: Donald H. Schuster (first academic description); in circulation earlier
first.where: A new ambiguous figure: a three-stick clevis. The American Journal of Psychology 77(4): 673, 1964

entries.effectEn: A figure with two rectangular prongs at one end and three round ones at the other, with no consistent way to get from one to the other.

mechanismEn.name: Figure and ground swap identity along the length of the object; resolving it requires an actual shift of fixation, which Schuster noted in 1964

entries.notesEn: The best example of an illusion with no findable author — folk knowledge that entered the literature sideways.

impl.notes: An SVG with a sliding occluder the visitor drags along the figure. Each end is locally coherent under the mask; the contradiction only exists when both are visible.

first.by: Valeria I. Petkova and H. Henrik Ehrsson
first.where: If I were you: perceptual illusion of body swapping. PLoS ONE 3(12): e3832

entries.effectEn: With a head-mounted display fed from a camera on another person head, and synchronised touch, participants experience the other body as their own — including shaking their own hand.

mechanismEn.name: Body ownership follows synchronised visual and tactile evidence, wherever that evidence points

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9.

impl.notes: Hardware-bound. Explanation and video only.

first.by: Wolfgang Köhler, as takete and baluba; Dimitri Uznadze reported a related observation in 1924
first.where: Köhler, Gestalt Psychology, Liveright, 1929; renamed bouba and kiki by Ramachandran and Hubbard, 2001

entries.effectEn: Shown a rounded blob and a spiky star and asked which is bouba and which is kiki, upwards of ninety per cent of people give the same answer, across most languages and writing systems.

mechanismEn.name: A non-arbitrary mapping between articulatory and acoustic properties of speech sounds and visual shape

entries.notesEn: Used as an argument that the earliest words were not arbitrary. The 2022 cross-cultural study found it holds across most but not all languages tested, which is the honest version of the claim.

impl.notes: Two shapes, two words, one click — and then show the running tally of everyone else answers. Trivial to build and it produces a real cross-linguistic dataset if the site asks which language the visitor thinks in. With Russian, Belarusian and English visitors that is worth doing properly.

first.where: La perception visuelle de l espace. Schleicher Frères, Paris, 1902

entries.effectEn: A straight edge running along two abutting triangles looks bent at the join.

mechanismEn.name: The apex angle of the adjacent wedge biases the judged orientation of the shared edge

impl.notes: Two triangles with a slider on wedge angle and a straightedge overlay toggle.

first.by: Laura A. Kelley and John A. Endler
first.where: Illusions promote mating success in great bowerbirds. Science 335(6066): 335–338

entries.effectEn: Male great bowerbirds arrange the objects on their display court by size, small at the front and large at the back, producing forced perspective for a female standing in the bower. Males who build better illusions mate more.

mechanismEn.name: A size gradient along the line of sight flattens the apparent depth of the court, and may make the male himself appear larger against it

entries.notesEn: The only entry in the catalogue whose author is not human. Also the answer to a question visitors ask constantly: do animals see illusions? Some do, some do not, and pigeons see the Ebbinghaus illusion backwards.

impl.notes: A WebGL court the visitor can rearrange, with a female-eye view alongside a top-down view. Being able to build the illusion yourself, and see the gradient that produces it, is the point.

first.by: Arthur G. Shapiro and Emily Knight
first.where: Where Has All the Motion Gone?, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2007 (third prize); the underlying analysis in Shapiro and Knight, Spatial Vision 21(3–5): 421–439, 2008

entries.effectEn: Four line segments moving in straight lines are seen as a square expanding and contracting.

mechanismEn.name: Aperture-problem again: local terminator motion is integrated into a global shape change that is not there

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9 as far as the record allows: a contest entry followed by a paper, which is the normal shape of a modern motion illusion.

impl.notes: Four segments with a toggle revealing their true independent trajectories.

first.by: Hugo Münsterberg (the figure); Richard L. Gregory and Priscilla Heard (1979, the name)
first.where: Münsterberg, Pseudoptics, Milton Bradley, 1894; Die verschobene Schachbrettfigur, Zeitschrift für Psychologie 15: 184–188, 1897; Pierce called it the kindergarten illusion in 1898; Gregory and Heard, Border locking and the Café Wall illusion, Perception 8(4): 365–380, 1979

entries.effectEn: Rows of offset light and dark tiles separated by thin grey mortar look wedge-shaped, although every row is parallel.

mechanismEn.name: Border locking: the mortar line is captured by the tile borders and tilts toward them, requiring the mortar luminance to lie between the tile luminances

entries.notesEn: The Bristol wall still exists. Note that the name is 1979 and the figure is 1894 — eighty-five years apart, which is a good illustration of why this catalogue separates the two.

impl.notes: Sliders on row offset, mortar thickness and mortar luminance. Setting mortar to pure black or pure white kills the effect, which is the cleanest possible demonstration of the border-locking account.

first.by: Jane E. Aspell, Olaf Blanke and colleagues
first.where: Turning body and self inside out: visualized heartbeats alter bodily self-consciousness and tactile perception. Psychological Science 24(12): 2445–2453

entries.effectEn: A silhouette of your own body, seen from behind, flashing in time with your own heartbeat, moves your sense of where you are toward it.

mechanismEn.name: Self-location is computed from signals pointing inward as well as outward; synchronising an external image with an internal rhythm binds the two

entries.notesEn: The finding that forced the taxonomy to add an interoceptive modality.

impl.notes: Needs a heart-rate sensor and a head-mounted display. Explanation only — but it earns the new modality, because nothing else in the catalogue is about signals from inside the body.

first.by: Ronald A. Rensink, J. Kevin O Regan and James J. Clark (the flicker paradigm)
first.where: To see or not to see: the need for attention to perceive changes in scenes. Psychological Science 8(5): 368–373

entries.effectEn: Two versions of a photograph alternating with a brief blank between them. A large object changes, appears or disappears, and observers can hunt for it for a minute without finding it.

mechanismEn.name: Without attention, scene representations are far sparser than they feel; the blank prevents the motion transient that would normally summon attention to the change

entries.notesEn: Pairs with inattentional blindness as the pair of exhibits that unsettle visitors most.

impl.notes: Our own photographs with our own edits, a proper flicker loop, a timer and a give-up button that highlights the change. Also worth building the gradual-change variant, where the change is made slowly with no blank at all and is even harder to see.

first.where: Essai analytique sur les facultés de l âme, 1760, describing his grandfather Charles Lullin

entries.effectEn: People losing their sight see vivid, detailed, silent hallucinations — patterns, faces, figures, buildings — while knowing perfectly well the visions are not real.

mechanismEn.name: Deafferentation: visual cortex deprived of input generates activity of its own, the visual analogue of tinnitus

impl.notes: Explanation only. Many patients never mention it for fear of being thought to be losing their mind; saying it is common and benign is the useful thing a page can do.

first.where: Cushion, and the related bulge figures, published on Kitaoka illusion pages from 1998

entries.effectEn: A regular checkerboard with small contrast elements at the corners bulges out of the plane.

mechanismEn.name: Border locking and orientation contrast, as in the café wall, accumulated across a 2D field

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9.

impl.notes: Procedural board with corner-element size and contrast on sliders, plus a straightedge overlay.

first.where: Published on the MIT Perceptual Science Group web page, 1995

entries.effectEn: Square A and square B on a chequerboard under a cylinder shadow are printed in exactly the same grey and look entirely different.

mechanismEn.name: The visual system discounts the illuminant: it is reporting surface reflectance, not luminance, and by that measure it is right
Anchoring within frameworks — the shadowed region is scaled to its own local white

entries.notesEn: The most effective single demonstration that vision reports reflectance, not light. Adelson point is that the visual system is not failing here; it is succeeding at a harder task.

impl.notes: Build it in WebGL rather than copying the bitmap: a real chequerboard, a real cylinder, a real shadow, and a camera the visitor can orbit. Then a wipe that connects A and B with a bar of the identical grey. Our own scene, our own geometry — and being able to move the light is something the original cannot do.

first.where: De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs. Pitois-Levrault, Paris, 1839

entries.effectEn: A staircase of uniform grey bands looks fluted: each band appears lighter at the edge next to a darker neighbour.

mechanismEn.name: Same lateral-inhibition machinery as Mach bands, applied at each step

impl.notes: Step wedge with a slider on step count and a masking tool that isolates one band, proving it is flat.

first.by: Petter Johansson, Lars Hall, Sverker Sikström and Andreas Olsson
first.where: Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in a simple decision task. Science 310(5745): 116–119

entries.effectEn: Choose between two faces, then be handed the one you rejected. Only about one person in eight notices — and the rest explain, fluently and at length, why they chose it.

mechanismEn.name: Introspective reports about ones own choices are constructed after the fact from the evidence available, not retrieved from a record of the decision

entries.notesEn: The memory and agency counterpart to change blindness, by the same logic and almost the same name.

impl.notes: Works in a browser with our own images and a swap the visitor cannot see. Only runs once per person, like the gorilla video, so it must not be labelled above the fold — and it needs an honest debrief the moment the trial ends.

first.where: Stereoskopie durch Farbendifferenz. Albrecht von Graefes Archiv für Ophthalmologie 31(3): 211–238

entries.effectEn: Saturated red and blue shapes on a dark ground appear to lie at different depths, usually red in front — but for some observers the order reverses.

mechanismEn.name: Chromatic aberration of the eye combined with a pupil displaced from the optical axis, so red and blue land at different disparities

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/colour. The depth comes from interocular disparity produced by chromatic aberration.

impl.notes: Red and blue text on black with a background-luminance slider; the depth order can be made to flip. Ask visitors which way it goes for them, because the reversal rate is high and interesting.

first.by: Kielan Yarrow, Patrick Haggard, Ron Heal, Peter Brown and John C. Rothwell
first.where: Illusory perceptions of space and time preserve cross-saccadic perceptual continuity. Nature 414(6861): 302–305

entries.effectEn: Glance at a clock with a ticking second hand and the first second seems to last far longer than a second. Measured at about 120 ms of extra apparent duration.

mechanismEn.name: The brain backdates the post-saccadic image to the start of the eye movement, filling the blind interval — so the first fixation is credited with time it did not have

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from temporal/time-perception. The stopped-clock illusion is saccade-triggered; it is a perisaccadic distortion of time and belongs with the others.

impl.notes: A digital clock in a corner of the screen and a fixation task elsewhere; the visitor saccades to it on a prompt. Works reasonably on a large screen. Also point them at a real analogue clock, which is the better version and costs nothing.

first.by: Charles Chubb, George Sperling and Joshua A. Solomon
first.where: Texture interactions determine perceived contrast. PNAS 86(23): 9631–9635

entries.effectEn: A textured patch looks lower in contrast when surrounded by high-contrast texture and higher when surrounded by a uniform field.

mechanismEn.name: Contrast gain control: the response to local contrast is normalised by surrounding contrast

entries.notesEn: Contrast is the dimension here, not lightness — worth keeping distinct in the taxonomy.

impl.notes: Two identical noise patches, surround contrast on a slider, and a matching task so the visitor produces a number.

first.by: Anthony M. Norcia (Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute)
first.where: Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2006

entries.effectEn: A pattern of rectangular panels that most people see as sixteen coffered doors. There are also sixteen circles, and most people cannot find them at first.

mechanismEn.name: Figure-ground assignment favours the closed rectangles; the circles are present but lose the competition for contour ownership

entries.notesEn: Went viral repeatedly, most recently in 2023, always without attribution.

impl.notes: Procedural — the pattern is a grid of line segments and is exactly specifiable. Add a highlight button that traces the circles, and a slider on segment length that shifts the balance between the two readings.

first.by: Edwin H. Land (the modern demonstrations); the phenomenon described much earlier by Helmholtz and Hering
first.where: Land, Experiments in color vision. Scientific American 200(5): 84–99

entries.effectEn: A surface keeps its apparent colour across enormous changes in the spectrum of the light falling on it — which is why every colour illusion in this section works at all.

mechanismEn.name: Retinex: lightness is computed separately in each waveband by comparing across the scene rather than reading absolute values

entries.notesEn: Catalogued as a capacity rather than an illusion, and the site should frame it that way: the illusions in this category are the seams where a normally invisible process shows.

impl.notes: A rendered scene with a physically meaningful illuminant slider and a readout of both the raw pixel colour and the surface reflectance. This is the explanatory backbone of the whole colour section rather than a standalone trick.

aka: filling in the afterimage after the image

first.by: Rob van Lier and Mark Vergeer (Radboud University)
first.where: Filling in the afterimage after the image, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2008 (first prize); Yuval Barkan and Hedva Spitzer, Colour Dove Illusion, BIOTY 2009 (second prize)

entries.effectEn: One multicoloured adapting image produces different afterimage colours depending on which outline shape is presented afterwards — the afterimage fills the shape you give it.

mechanismEn.name: Afterimage colour is assigned to surfaces bounded by contours, so contours presented after adaptation still control it

entries.notesEn: Strong evidence that afterimages are not simply retinal residue.

impl.notes: Shares the timing machinery with negative-afterimage; the addition is a set of outlines the visitor picks between after adaptation.

first.by: Paul A. Kolers and Michael von Grünau
first.where: Shape and color in apparent motion. Vision Research 16(4): 329–335

entries.effectEn: A red dot flashed, then a green dot flashed nearby, is seen as one dot moving — and changing colour partway across, before the green dot has appeared.

mechanismEn.name: The percept is constructed after both stimuli arrive; Dennett used it to argue there is no single moment at which perception happens

entries.notesEn: The philosophically loaded one: it is hard to describe the percept without saying the brain reported the future.

impl.notes: Two dots, two colours, an interval slider. The effect has a narrow timing window, so the demo needs precise frame timing and should show the measured interstimulus interval in milliseconds.

first.by: Celeste McCollough (the first and defining case)
first.where: Color adaptation of edge-detectors in the human visual system. Science 149(3688): 1115–1116

entries.effectEn: An aftereffect that appears only when the test stimulus shares a property with the adapting one — colour contingent on orientation, motion contingent on colour, and so on.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation in cells jointly tuned to two dimensions; the extreme persistence suggests error-correction learning rather than fatigue

impl.notes: Umbrella exhibit around the McCollough effect, carrying the same persistence warning.

first.where: The Bakerian Lecture — Contributions to the physiology of vision, Part the second. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 142: 1–17

entries.effectEn: Objects look smaller when the eyes are converged more than the viewing distance requires — which is why autostereogram scenes often look miniature.

mechanismEn.name: Vergence provides a distance signal; over-convergence signals a nearer distance, and perceived size is scaled down accordingly

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/geometric-size. Vergence is a binocular signal.

impl.notes: Best shown inside the autostereogram exhibit, where visitors meet it anyway.

first.by: Documented in the aviation medicine literature of the 1940s
first.where: Graybiel and colleagues, Journal of Aviation Medicine, from 1946 onward

entries.effectEn: Move your head during a sustained turn and the world tumbles violently in a direction that has nothing to do with what the aircraft is doing.

mechanismEn.name: Head movement during rotation stimulates semicircular canals in a plane other than the one adapted to, producing a strong sensation of rotation about a third axis

entries.notesEn: A named cause of fatal accidents in instrument flight. The aviation framing is not decoration; it is why these illusions were studied at all.

impl.notes: A rotating office chair reproduces it, and the site can say so with a safety note — do it seated, with someone present. No browser version exists and none should be faked.

first.by: Tom N. Cornsweet; earlier observations by Kenneth Craik (1940s) and Vivian O Brien (1958)
first.where: Cornsweet, Visual Perception. Academic Press, 1970

entries.effectEn: Two regions of identical luminance look different because of what happens in a narrow gradient between them. Cover the join and they snap to being equal.

mechanismEn.name: Edge information propagates into the flat regions — the visual system reconstructs surfaces from their borders

entries.notesEn: The best evidence for the idea that vision codes edges and infers the rest, which is also why image compression can get away with the same trick.

impl.notes: The occluder is the demo: a draggable strip the visitor puts over the central gradient, at which point the two halves visibly become one grey. Add a luminance readout so it is a measurement, not a claim.

first.by: A special case of the light-from-above prior; no separate first description located
first.where: Ramachandran, Perception of shape from shading. Nature 331: 163–166, 1988

entries.effectEn: Impact craters in a photograph appear as raised domes when the image is rotated so the light comes from below.

mechanismEn.name: Light-from-above prior applied to a scene whose real illumination came from another direction

entries.notesEn: A practical nuisance in planetary science: images are conventionally published with illumination from the left for exactly this reason.

impl.notes: A public-domain lunar or Martian photograph with a rotation slider. NASA imagery is public domain, which makes this one of the few entries where we can use a real photograph without a licensing problem.

first.where: Minnaert 1954

entries.effectEn: Shafts of light appearing to radiate from the sun in a fan. The shafts are parallel; the fan is perspective.

mechanismEn.name: Parallel beams converging at a vanishing point, made visible by scattering. A rare case where the optical cause and a perspective misjudgement stack

entries.notesEn: Sits on the boundary: the beams are physically there, their apparent divergence is perspective. Worth using on the site to show the boundary is not always sharp.

first.by: Wilhelm Korte (first description); Herman Bouma (1970, the quantitative law)
first.where: Korte, Über die Gestaltauffassung im indirekten Sehen, Zeitschrift für Psychologie 93: 17–82, 1923; Ehlers 1936; Bouma, Nature 226(5241): 177–178, 1970

entries.effectEn: A letter easily read in peripheral vision becomes unreadable when flanked by other letters — though you can still see that something is there.

mechanismEn.name: Features are pooled over a region that grows with eccentricity; Bouma law puts the critical spacing at roughly half the eccentricity

entries.notesEn: The main limit on peripheral reading speed, and the reason the automated Wikipedia pass matched this id to a disambiguation page about crowds.

impl.notes: Fixation cross plus a target letter at adjustable eccentricity with adjustable flankers. The visitor can measure their own critical spacing and check Bouma law against it — a real replication in about a minute.

first.where: Curvature blindness illusion. i-Perception 8(6)

entries.effectEn: Identical sine waves are seen as smooth curves on some backgrounds and as sharp zigzags on others. The only difference is where the line changes contrast polarity.

mechanismEn.name: Contrast-polarity reversal at the turning points is read as a corner; a corner interpretation dominates a curve interpretation when both are available

entries.notesEn: One of the few genuinely new geometric illusions of the last decade.

impl.notes: Fully specified in an open-access paper: sliders on wave amplitude, background luminance and where along the wave the polarity switches. Moving the switch point off the turning point kills the illusion instantly.

first.by: Arthur G. Shapiro, Zhong-Lin Lu, Emily Knight and Robert Ennis
first.where: Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2009 (first prize); published as PLoS ONE 5(10): e13296 (2010)

entries.effectEn: A spinning ball moving on a smooth path appears to break sharply when the gaze shifts from central to peripheral vision.

mechanismEn.name: Central vision tracks position and spin separately; peripheral vision combines them, so the perceived trajectory changes at the moment of transition

entries.notesEn: The best example in the catalogue of an illusion that explains something people argued about for a century — whether a curveball really breaks.

impl.notes: A spinning disc on a straight descent with a fixation point the visitor can move. The break appears exactly when they stop looking at the ball.

first.by: Frank A. Geldard and Carl E. Sherrick (Princeton)
first.where: The cutaneous rabbit: a perceptual illusion. Science 178(4057): 178–179

entries.effectEn: Tap the wrist three times, then the elbow three times, quickly. The taps are felt hopping evenly up the forearm, landing in places nothing touched.

mechanismEn.name: Location is assigned after the fact, using the later taps to reinterpret the earlier ones — a tactile postdiction

entries.notesEn: The clearest tactile evidence that perception is not built in real time: where you felt a tap depends on what happened next.

impl.notes: Needs two tappers at controlled timing — feasible with two small vibration motors on a microcontroller, or with a patient partner and a pencil. Ship the protocol with the timing (roughly 40–80 ms between taps) and a diagram. A phone with two haptic points would work, but no phone has two.

first.where: Photograph published in Life magazine, 1965; adopted by the perception literature as the canonical closure demonstration

entries.effectEn: A field of black and white blotches with no discernible object in it. Once you see the Dalmatian sniffing the ground, you can never fail to see it again.

mechanismEn.name: Perceptual closure from fragmentary evidence, and the irreversibility of it: the organisation, once found, is applied automatically thereafter

impl.notes: Cannot reuse the copyrighted photograph. Generate our own from a silhouette plus procedural blotch noise, with a reveal-outline button and a timer of how long the visitor took. Shares the one-way-door design with Mooney faces and sine-wave speech — those three should be one exhibit about knowledge changing perception permanently.

first.where: Letter in Revue Philosophique de la France et de l Étranger, 1876

entries.effectEn: A powerful sense of having lived through the present moment before, combined with the certain knowledge that you have not.

mechanismEn.name: A familiarity signal generated without a matching recollection; the metacognitive system registers the mismatch, which is why the experience feels uncanny rather than simply like remembering

entries.notesEn: The only entry in the catalogue that is defined entirely by a subjective report with no stimulus. Worth saying so — it marks the edge of what this catalogue can even be about.

impl.notes: Cannot be induced reliably on demand outside a laboratory. Explanation only, with the virtual-reality scene-matching studies described.

first.where: Note sur certaines illusions d optique. Bulletins de l Académie Royale des Sciences, Lettres et Beaux-Arts de Belgique 19: 195–216

entries.effectEn: A disc looks larger when a close-fitting ring is drawn around it and smaller when the ring is far outside it.

mechanismEn.name: Same contour-proximity machinery as the Ebbinghaus illusion, with the ring acting as a single inducer

entries.notesEn: The most practically cited of the size illusions: portion size on a large plate is systematically underestimated.

impl.notes: One disc, one ring, slider on ring radius. Worth a second panel showing the plate-size version, since this is the illusion behind the advice to eat off smaller plates.

first.by: Philippe G. Schyns and Aude Oliva
first.where: Dr. Angry and Mr. Smile: when categorization flexibly modifies the perception of faces in rapid visual presentations. Cognition 69(3): 243–265

entries.effectEn: Two faces side by side, one angry and one smiling — that swap expressions when you step back from the screen.

mechanismEn.name: Each face carries one expression in high spatial frequencies and the other in low; viewing distance selects which band is resolvable

impl.notes: A preset of the hybrid-image tool built from our own expression photographs, with a zoom control standing in for distance.

first.by: James Deese; revived by Henry L. Roediger III and Kathleen B. McDermott in 1995
first.where: Deese, Journal of Experimental Psychology 58(1): 17–22, 1959; Roediger and McDermott, JEP:LMC 21(4): 803–814, 1995

entries.effectEn: Learn a list of related words — bed, rest, awake, tired, dream — and confidently remember a word that was never on it. Sleep.

mechanismEn.name: Retrieval reconstructs from gist rather than replaying a record; the unpresented lure fits the gist better than some of the words that were there

entries.notesEn: The memory counterpart to the perceptual illusions: the same demonstration that what you get is constructed, not recorded.

impl.notes: Timed word list, a distractor task, then a recognition test including the critical lure. The confidence rating is essential: people are not merely wrong, they are sure. Needs lists built for Russian and Belarusian, not translated from English — associative structure does not survive translation, and getting that right is real linguistic work.

first.where: Dual Axis Illusion, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2019 (first prize)

entries.effectEn: A spinning ring can be seen rotating about the vertical axis or the horizontal one, and switches when you follow a different part of it.

mechanismEn.name: A bistable structure-from-motion figure with two equally valid rigid interpretations

impl.notes: Pure procedural line drawing — well within reach and a good candidate for an early build, with a cue overlay that biases the visitor toward one reading.

first.where: Fliegende Blätter, 23 October 1892, p. 147, captioned Welche Thiere gleichen einander am meisten?

entries.effectEn: One drawing, a duck facing left or a rabbit facing right, switching without warning.

mechanismEn.name: One image, two object hypotheses of equal strength; attention to the beak or the ears biases the outcome

entries.notesEn: Wittgenstein used it to argue that seeing is already interpretation, which is as good a summary of this whole catalogue as anyone has written.

impl.notes: The 1892 original is public domain, which is rare and useful. Add a morph slider between an unambiguous duck and an unambiguous rabbit so the visitor can find their own crossover point.

first.where: Explaining lightness illusions. Perception 30(9): 1031–1046

entries.effectEn: Identical grey disks in two grids of bars look markedly different in lightness, and the difference depends on which disks group with which bars rather than on what surrounds them.

mechanismEn.name: Double anchoring: lightness is computed within a perceptual group, so remote luminances matter only when grouping lets them

entries.notesEn: Found only through the German-language index. It is absent from the English list the project started from.

impl.notes: Procedural grid with a grouping-strength slider. Belongs beside White illusion and the Benary cross as the third member of the belongingness argument.

first.by: Christopher D. Blair, Gideon P. Caplovitz and Ryan E. B. Mruczek
first.where: Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2014 (first prize); published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 9: 77 (2015)

entries.effectEn: The Ebbinghaus illusion becomes several times stronger when the surrounding circles change size while the whole array drifts across the screen.

mechanismEn.name: Motion and dynamic context defeat the mechanisms that normally limit contextual size effects

entries.notesEn: A good argument for building the catalogue interactively rather than as a picture gallery: this illusion barely exists as a still image.

impl.notes: Extends the static Ebbinghaus demo with two toggles — inducer pulsing and array drift — so the visitor can add each factor and watch the effect grow.

first.where: Titchener, Experimental Psychology: A Manual of Laboratory Practice, Vol. I. Macmillan, 1901

entries.effectEn: A circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller than an identical circle surrounded by small ones.

mechanismEn.name: Size contrast against the surrounding context
Contour proximity rather than inducer size as such — the nearer the ring, the stronger the effect

entries.notesEn: Famous second life in the perception-versus-action debate: Aglioti et al. reported grasping is immune to the illusion, Franz and others reported it is not. Doherty et al. 2010 found young children are less fooled than adults.

impl.notes: Both centre discs drawn from one variable; drag to resize and read off the point of subjective equality. The dynamic version (Mruczek et al., BIOTY 2014) is worth building as a second mode: the effect gets much stronger when the inducers move.

first.where: Über Abwandlungen der L. Hermannschen Helligkeitserscheinung. Zeitschrift für Psychologie 150: 83–91

entries.effectEn: Radial line segments stopping short of a common centre produce a bright disc with a visible edge, brighter than the white page.

mechanismEn.name: Illusory contour formation from line terminations
Adding coloured inner segments turns it into neon colour spreading

entries.notesEn: Note the name collision with the Ehrenstein square distortion in geometric-shape — the site must disambiguate or visitors will assume a duplicate.

impl.notes: Sliders on gap size and line count; one toggle recolours the inner segments and slides the whole thing into neon colour spreading, which makes the family relationship visible.

first.where: Probleme der ganzheitspsychologischen Wahrnehmungslehre. Johann Ambrosius Barth, Leipzig, 1954

entries.effectEn: The sides of a square drawn across concentric circles bow inward.

mechanismEn.name: Same orientation-contrast family as Hering, Wundt and Orbison

entries.notesEn: Two different figures carry the Ehrenstein name and the catalogue had merged their citations. Cross-reference ehrenstein-illusion in contours-filling.

impl.notes: Preset of the Orbison renderer; kept separate so the naming collision can be explained on the page.

first.where: Größenverhältnisse der Nachbilder. Klinische Monatsblätter für Augenheilkunde 19: 443–450

entries.effectEn: An afterimage projected onto a distant wall looks huge; projected onto your hand it looks small. The retinal image never changes.

mechanismEn.name: Perceived size equals retinal size scaled by perceived distance — the same rule that produces size constancy, applied to a stimulus with no real distance at all

entries.notesEn: Probably the cleanest single piece of evidence for the size-distance scaling account of the moon illusion.

impl.notes: An adapting patch and then instructions to look at surfaces at different distances in the room. One of the few exhibits that deliberately sends the visitor away from the screen, which is a good thing to do once.

first.by: Isia Leviant (as a painting); published by Leviant (1996)
first.where: Painted 1981; Does brain-power make Enigma spin? Proceedings of the Royal Society B 263(1373): 997–1001, 1996

entries.effectEn: Coloured rings laid over a dense radial line pattern fill with rapid streaming motion, like fluid circulating in channels.

mechanismEn.name: Driven by microsaccades — the streaming speed tracks microsaccade rate almost perfectly

entries.notesEn: An artwork that turned out to be a precise instrument: it made the contribution of microsaccades to perception measurable.

impl.notes: Procedural radial lines plus concentric annuli with a slider on line density and ring width. Our own geometry, not Leviant painting, which is under copyright.

first.where: Lithograph, first printed May 1958

entries.effectEn: A two-storey pavilion whose upper floor is turned ninety degrees from the lower one while sharing the same eight columns.

mechanismEn.name: Column connections are drawn front-to-back and back-to-front alternately; each is locally plausible

entries.notesEn: Copyright status matters for this whole sub-category and should be stated in the section introduction.

impl.notes: Escher works are in copyright until 2043 (he died in 1972), so we cannot reproduce the lithograph. We can build our own pavilion using the same column trick — a different building, the same impossibility. That is the honest and the more interesting route.

first.where: Lithograph, first printed October 1961

entries.effectEn: Water runs downhill along a zigzag channel and arrives at the top of the fall that feeds it, driving a mill forever.

mechanismEn.name: Three Penrose triangles chained so that the accumulated height around the circuit is inconsistent

impl.notes: Same copyright constraint. Build our own watercourse from tribars with animated flow, and orbit to reveal the break.

first.where: On some of the disorders of sleep. Virginia Medical Monthly 2: 769–781, 1876

entries.effectEn: A deafening bang, gunshot or crash inside the head at the moment of falling asleep. Painless, harmless, and terrifying the first time.

mechanismEn.name: A misfire in the brainstem sequence that normally shuts down sensory systems at sleep onset — a burst rather than a fade

entries.notesEn: The same Silas Weir Mitchell who named the phantom limb. Two entries in this catalogue from one nineteenth-century neurologist.

impl.notes: Explanation only. Like Charles Bonnet syndrome, the useful thing a page can do is say that it is common and benign, which is what sufferers are usually not told.

first.by: Jacques Ninio and Kent A. Stevens
first.where: Variations on the Hermann grid: an extinction illusion. Perception 29(10): 1209–1217

entries.effectEn: Twelve black dots sit at the intersections of a grey grid and you can never see more than a few at once.

mechanismEn.name: Peripheral crowding and filling-in: the grid texture is completed over the dots outside the fovea

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. Went viral in 2016 as the twelve-dot illusion with no attribution attached — exactly the failure this catalogue exists to fix.

impl.notes: Grid with dot count and contrast sliders, plus a counter asking the visitor how many dots they can hold at once. The answer is never twelve.

first.where: Looking at upside-down faces. Journal of Experimental Psychology 81(1): 141–145

entries.effectEn: Turning a photograph upside down hurts face recognition far more than it hurts recognition of houses or aeroplanes.

mechanismEn.name: Faces are processed configurally, as wholes, and that machinery is orientation-specific

entries.notesEn: The foundation under the Thatcher effect and the composite face effect.

impl.notes: A matching task with faces and non-face objects at both orientations, timed. This is a real experiment and produces the visitor own inversion cost in milliseconds — more convincing than any assertion.

first.where: Cognitive effects of false heart-rate feedback. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 4(4): 400–408

entries.effectEn: Play someone a heartbeat they believe is their own, speed it up, and they find the photograph they are looking at more attractive — or the exercise they are doing more exhausting.

mechanismEn.name: Emotion and effort are inferred partly from bodily state; substitute a false signal and the inference follows it rather than the body

impl.notes: A browser version is possible and unusually cheap: a heartbeat sound the visitor is told is theirs, varied in rate, with a rating task. It requires a deception and therefore an immediate, unambiguous debrief — say plainly that the sound was never their pulse.

first.where: Synsoplevede Figurer. Doctoral thesis, Copenhagen, 1915

entries.effectEn: The visual field is always split into an object that owns its contour and a background that extends behind it. The split can be reversed, and only one side is ever the object.

mechanismEn.name: Contour ownership assigned by cues including convexity, size, symmetry, enclosure and familiarity

entries.notesEn: The principle that makes Rubin vase, the coffer illusion and the Benary cross a single family.

impl.notes: A demonstration with one cue per slider — convexity, symmetry, area, enclosure — showing how each biases which region becomes the object. More useful than another ambiguous picture.

first.by: Donald M. MacKay; rediscovered and named by Romi Nijhawan (1994)
first.where: MacKay, Nature 181(4607): 507–508, 1958; Nijhawan, Motion extrapolation in catching. Nature 370(6487): 256–257, 1994

entries.effectEn: A flash presented exactly alongside a moving object is seen lagging behind it.

mechanismEn.name: Motion extrapolation: the visual system predicts forward to compensate for its own latency
Postdiction: the percept of the flash position is determined by what happens after it
Differential latency between flashed and moving stimuli

entries.notesEn: Origin resolved in W9. The mechanism remains genuinely open — prediction versus postdiction versus differential latency — and the site should present the argument rather than a verdict.

impl.notes: A rotating bar with a flashed segment and a nulling control: the visitor adjusts the flash offset until it looks aligned, and the site records the offset in milliseconds. Requires frame-accurate timing; measure and display the actual frame interval rather than assuming 60 Hz.

first.by: Jason M. Tangen, Sean C. Murphy and Matthew B. Thompson
first.where: The flashed face distortion effect. Perception 40(5): 628–630

entries.effectEn: A stream of ordinary faces flashed in pairs beside a fixation point turns grotesque and deformed within seconds. Stop and look at any one of them and it is perfectly normal.

mechanismEn.name: Peripheral face processing plus rapid adaptation: each face is coded relative to the previous one, and the differences are exaggerated

entries.notesEn: The strongest illusion in the catalogue relative to how simple its stimulus is, and a good demonstration that peripheral vision is not a low-resolution copy of central vision but something qualitatively different.

impl.notes: Needs a set of aligned face photographs we have rights to — the alignment on eye position is what makes it work. A generated face set is a legitimate route and sidesteps the rights problem entirely. Controls for presentation rate and eccentricity.

first.where: On a distinct form of transient hemiopsia. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 160: 247–264

entries.effectEn: A shimmering crescent of zigzag lines expands slowly across the visual field over twenty minutes, leaving a blind area behind it. Roughly a fifth of migraine sufferers see it.

mechanismEn.name: A wave of cortical spreading depression crossing visual cortex at about 3 mm per minute; the zigzag geometry reflects the orientation columns the wave passes through
mechanismEn.by: Lashley, Milner, and the modern account

entries.notesEn: A rare case where an illusion is also a direct readout of cortical geometry — the shape of the percept tells you how the cortex is laid out.

impl.notes: Simulatable and genuinely useful: an expanding zigzag arc over a fixation point, at the documented speed, from Airy own drawings. People who have never had one cannot picture it, and people who have had one often cannot describe it. A clear warning that it may be uncomfortable for migraine sufferers is required.

first.where: Some considerations on the mechanism of directional hearing. Doctoral thesis, Delft, 1960

entries.effectEn: A tone that starts abruptly in one loudspeaker and then fades across to another is heard as staying in the first speaker — even after the first has been switched off entirely.

mechanismEn.name: Localisation is dominated by the onset transient; for a steady tone in a reverberant room there is no reliable later cue, so the initial assignment simply persists

entries.notesEn: A good example of an illusion that depends on the room, not only on the listener.

impl.notes: Needs real loudspeakers in a real room; it does not work on headphones and it barely works without reverberation. Present as an explanation with a diagram and be honest that this one cannot be delivered through a web page.

first.where: A new visual illusion of direction. British Journal of Psychology 2(3): 307–320

entries.effectEn: Overlapping arcs of twisted cord read as a continuous spiral. They are concentric circles.

mechanismEn.name: Local orientation signals from the twisted-cord elements are integrated along the contour and outvote the global circularity

entries.notesEn: Fraser generalised it: the same twisted-cord trick makes letters lean and chequered grounds warp.

impl.notes: Generate the twisted cord procedurally so a slider can sweep the element tilt through zero, where the spiral snaps back into circles. Tracing one circle with the cursor is the proof.

first.by: Alastair Fraser and Kimerly J. Wilcox
first.where: Perception of illusory movement. Nature 281: 565–566

entries.effectEn: Repeated dark-to-light gradients appear to slide continuously, like an escalator.

mechanismEn.name: The asymmetric luminance gradient again; Kitaoka has since catalogued optimised variants up to Type V

entries.notesEn: Worth keeping separate: this is the priority claim that Rotating Snakes rests on.

impl.notes: Preset of the peripheral-drift renderer with the original gradient profile.

first.where: The Freezing Rotation Illusion, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2006 (first prize)

entries.effectEn: A rotating pattern appears to stop rotating when a second motion component is added, even though it never slows.

mechanismEn.name: Competing motion signals cancel in the perceived rotation while the physical rotation continues

impl.notes: Needs the two motion components separable by slider so the cancellation point can be found.

first.where: Frequency doubling in visual responses. Journal of the Optical Society of America 56(11): 1628–1633

entries.effectEn: A low-spatial-frequency grating counterphase-flickering at a high rate appears to have twice as many bars as it does.

mechanismEn.name: A nonlinear, probably magnocellular, response that rectifies the signal and so doubles its apparent spatial frequency

entries.notesEn: One of the very few illusions with a routine clinical use: frequency-doubling perimetry screens for glaucoma with it.

impl.notes: Canvas grating with counterphase flicker, sliders on spatial frequency and temporal rate. Needs measured frame timing. The visitor can count bars and be wrong by a factor of two, which is unusually crisp for a perceptual demo.

first.by: Bigna Lenggenhager, Tej Tadi, Thomas Metzinger and Olaf Blanke
first.where: Video ergo sum: manipulating bodily self-consciousness. Science 317(5841): 1096–1099

entries.effectEn: Watching your own back being stroked from three metres behind, through a head-mounted display, while feeling the stroking, drifts your sense of where you are toward the body you can see.

mechanismEn.name: The same multisensory reconciliation as the rubber hand, applied to the whole body — self-location follows the visual body

entries.notesEn: Split from the Ehrsson out-of-body illusion in W13 after an adversarial audit caught the conflation.

impl.notes: Needs a head-mounted display, a camera and a second person. WebXR could in principle do it but the hardware requirement puts it outside what the site can deliver. Explanation, diagram and video only, and say so.

first.where: Funneling in the nervous system and its role in loudness and sensation intensity on the skin. JASA 30(5): 399–412

entries.effectEn: Two vibrators buzzing at once on nearby skin are felt as one buzz, in a place neither is touching. Change their relative strength and the phantom slides between them.

mechanismEn.name: Lateral inhibition in the somatosensory system funnels the two inputs into a single localised percept at their weighted centre

entries.notesEn: The reason a phone with two motors can place a sensation between them, and the foundation of the vibrotactile-display industry.

impl.notes: Two vibration motors and a microcontroller. Not a browser demo, but it is the basis of most haptic wearables, so the explanation carries real engineering weight.

first.where: Die Farbenkonstanz der Sehdinge, in Handbuch der normalen und pathologischen Physiologie, Bd. 12. Springer, 1929

entries.effectEn: A black disc lit by a hidden spotlight in a dark room looks white — until a genuinely white piece of paper is held next to it, at which point it collapses back to black.

mechanismEn.name: Anchoring: the highest luminance in a framework is taken as white, so an isolated disc has nothing to be dark relative to

entries.notesEn: The physical demonstration is dramatic and the screen version is not. Worth being explicit about that rather than pretending.

impl.notes: Genuinely hard in a browser, because it depends on real illumination. A WebGL room with a controllable spotlight and a reference card the visitor can drag into the beam is the closest honest approximation, and the page should say it is an approximation.

first.where: Some new luminance-gradient effects. Perception 28(7): 835–838

entries.effectEn: A white region surrounded by converging luminance gradients looks like a light source rather than a white surface.

mechanismEn.name: Converging luminance gradients are the optical signature of glare, so the enclosed region is assigned a luminosity that exceeds the physical white of the page

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/brightness-contrast. A glare percept is a judgement that a surface is self-luminous, which is a material attribution.

impl.notes: Shares a renderer with the Asahi illusion.

first.by: Diana Deutsch, Kamil Hamaoui and Trevor Henthorn
first.where: The glissando illusion and handedness. Neuropsychologia 45(13): 2981–2988

entries.effectEn: A synthesised oboe tone alternating between the ears, with a glissando that switches between them, is heard as the oboe staying put while the glide travels around the head in a way it never does.

mechanismEn.name: The steady tone and the glide are grouped as separate streams and localised independently

impl.notes: Headphones mandatory. Needs an oboe-like synthesised timbre, which Web Audio can do with additive synthesis; per-channel solo again.

first.by: Long observed from mountains and aircraft; the physics resisted explanation into the twenty-first century
first.where: Minnaert, Light and Colour in the Open Air, 1954

entries.effectEn: Coloured rings around the shadow of your own head, cast on cloud or fog below.

mechanismEn.name: Backscattering from small water droplets by a surface-wave mechanism; a full explanation required Mie theory and was still being refined in the 2000s

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: A spatial frequency dependent grating-induction effect. Vision Research 22(1): 119–134

entries.effectEn: A uniform grey strip running through a sinusoidal grating takes on a counterphase grating of its own. There is no luminance variation in the strip at all.

mechanismEn.name: Contrast induction from the surrounding grating, tuned to spatial frequency — the effect that Blakeslee and McCourt multiscale filtering models were built to explain alongside White illusion

entries.notesEn: Belongs next to White illusion and the Benary cross in the lightness argument; it is the case the filtering models handle best.

impl.notes: Canvas grating with a grey strip, sliders on spatial frequency and strip height. A luminance probe along the strip proving it is flat is the necessary control.

first.by: Paola Bressan, Luigi Garlaschelli and Monica Barracano (the explanation)
first.where: Antigravity hills are visual illusions. Psychological Science 14(5): 441–449

entries.effectEn: A downhill road looks uphill, and a car left out of gear appears to roll up it.

mechanismEn.name: With the true horizon obscured, slope is judged against misleading local references — sloping trees, walls and roadsides

entries.notesEn: Belarus has at least one such site; worth a local note on the page if it can be verified.

impl.notes: A WebGL road with independent controls for true slope, horizon visibility and the tilt of roadside objects. Being able to make a genuinely downhill road look uphill, then reveal the horizon, is a clean reproduction of the paper.

first.by: Long known to sailors; popularised by Jules Verne, Le Rayon vert, 1882
first.where: Minnaert 1954; Lynch and Livingston 2001

entries.effectEn: A vivid green spot at the upper rim of the sun for a second or two at sunset, which many people spend years failing to see and then dismiss as a myth.

mechanismEn.name: Atmospheric dispersion separates the sun images by colour, and the green image is the last to set once the blue has been scattered away

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

aka: red strawberries that are not red

first.where: Published on Kitaoka illusion pages and social media, 2017

entries.effectEn: A photograph of strawberries containing no pixel whose hue is red still looks unmistakably red.

mechanismEn.name: Colour constancy: the cyan cast is attributed to the illuminant and discounted, leaving the strawberries their remembered colour

entries.notesEn: Pairs naturally with the dress: one shows constancy working, the other shows it splitting a population in two.

impl.notes: Shoot our own still life, apply our own cyan cast, ship an eyedropper that reads out hue on hover. The measurement is the exhibit — without it the visitor has only our word for it.

first.by: Recorded for centuries; systematised in the atmospheric-optics literature
first.where: Minnaert 1954; Lynch and Livingston 2001

entries.effectEn: A ring of light exactly 22 degrees around the sun or moon, with the sky inside it noticeably darker.

mechanismEn.name: Refraction through the 60-degree prism faces of randomly oriented hexagonal ice crystals, with a minimum deviation of 22 degrees

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: Minnaert 1954

entries.effectEn: Distant objects rippling and boiling above hot ground.

mechanismEn.name: Turbulent cells of different refractive index crossing the line of sight; the same effect that makes stars twinkle

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: An experimental study of apparent behavior. The American Journal of Psychology 57(2): 243–259

entries.effectEn: Two triangles and a circle move around a rectangle for ninety seconds, and observers see bullying, courtship, fear and escape. Almost nobody describes it in geometric terms.

mechanismEn.name: Motion kinematics alone — speed changes, contingency, self-propulsion — are sufficient to trigger the machinery for reading intention

entries.notesEn: Pairs with biological motion: one shows animacy read from a human skeleton, the other from three shapes with no bodies at all.

impl.notes: Animate our own shapes on our own trajectories, ask the visitor to describe what happened in a free-text box, then show what other visitors wrote. The distribution of spontaneous narratives is the result, and collecting it in three languages would be a genuinely new observation.

first.where: Beiträge zur Physiologie, Erstes Heft: Vom Ortsinne der Netzhaut. Wilhelm Engelmann, 1861

entries.effectEn: Two straight parallel lines look bowed outward when drawn over a radial fan.

mechanismEn.name: Orientation contrast at each intersection, accumulating along the line
Perceiving the near future: the radial pattern signals forward motion and the visual system pre-compensates for the geometry it expects next

entries.notesEn: Pairs naturally with the Wundt illusion, which is the same geometry inverted.

impl.notes: Radial fan with a slider on ray count, plus the Wundt inversion as a second tab (rays crossing outside the lines bow them inward).

first.where: Eine Erscheinung simultanen Contrastes. Pflügers Archiv für die gesamte Physiologie 3: 13–15

entries.effectEn: Grey smudges appear at the intersections of a grid of white streets on black, everywhere except where you look.

mechanismEn.name: Retinal lateral inhibition: a receptive field at an intersection receives more surround light
The retinal account fails — the illusion disappears if the streets are made wavy, which receptive fields cannot explain; cortical orientation-tuned cells are the current candidate

entries.notesEn: The best example in the catalogue of a textbook explanation that survived decades after the evidence against it.

impl.notes: Grid with sliders on street width and spacing, plus the decisive control: a toggle that makes the streets sinusoidal. The smudges vanish, and the textbook explanation goes with them. That control is the reason to build this one.

first.where: The Intelligent Eye. Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1970

entries.effectEn: The inside of a face mask looks like a normal outward-bulging face, and appears to turn and follow you as you move.

mechanismEn.name: A very strong prior that faces are convex overrides stereo and shading evidence to the contrary

entries.notesEn: People with schizophrenia are markedly less susceptible, which made the illusion into a clinical measure. Mention carefully and cite, since the finding is often overstated.

impl.notes: WebGL concave face with a lighting control and an orbit control. The illusion is weaker on a flat screen than in person, so pair it with a printable paper dragon template — the physical version is far stronger and we should say so rather than oversell the digital one.

first.by: Aude Oliva, Antonio Torralba and Philippe G. Schyns
first.where: Hybrid images. ACM Transactions on Graphics 25(3): 527–532

entries.effectEn: One image shows one thing close up and a completely different thing from across the room, or when you squint.

mechanismEn.name: High spatial frequencies from one image combined with low frequencies from another; viewing distance decides which band the visual system can resolve

impl.notes: Build the filter pipeline ourselves — Gaussian low-pass on one image, high-pass on the other, with a cutoff slider — and let visitors upload two of their own images. A zoom-out button substitutes for walking backwards. This is the best candidate in the catalogue for a tool visitors will actually use.

first.by: Alfred Maury coined the term hypnagogique
first.where: Des hallucinations hypnagogiques. Annales Médico-Psychologiques 11: 26–40

entries.effectEn: Vivid images, faces, patterns, voices and falling sensations at the edge of sleep, experienced as perceived rather than imagined.

mechanismEn.name: Sensory cortex active while external input is gated out and reality-monitoring is offline

impl.notes: Explanation only. Worth pairing with the Tetris effect, where a repeated daytime task reappears at sleep onset, because that version is reproducible at home.

first.by: Daniel M. Wegner and Thalia Wheatley
first.where: Apparent mental causation: sources of the experience of will. American Psychologist 54(7): 480–492

entries.effectEn: People report having intended an action that was in fact produced by someone else, provided a matching thought arrived at the right moment beforehand.

mechanismEn.name: The feeling of willing is an inference from priority, consistency and exclusivity — the thought came first, it matched, and nothing else obviously caused it — rather than a direct readout of causation

entries.notesEn: The strongest argument in the catalogue that the sense of authorship is itself a perception, and therefore fallible in the same way as any other.

impl.notes: The original needs a confederate. A software version can approximate it: the visitor moves a cursor that is partly under program control, with primes timed against the programmed movements, and reports afterwards how much of each movement felt like theirs. Debrief immediately and explicitly — this experiment works by deceiving the participant.

first.where: The illusion of control. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 32(2): 311–328

entries.effectEn: People value a lottery ticket they chose themselves more than one handed to them, and throw dice harder for high numbers. Control is felt where none exists.

mechanismEn.name: Cues associated with skill — choice, familiarity, involvement, competition — are imported into judgements about purely chance outcomes

impl.notes: A button that does nothing, a light that comes on randomly, and a rating afterwards of how much control the visitor felt. Vary whether they chose when to press. The measured confidence in a disconnected button is the exhibit.

first.by: George A. Miller and J. C. R. Licklider
first.where: The intelligibility of interrupted speech. JASA 22(2): 167–173

entries.effectEn: Cut a gap in a tone and fill it with noise, and the tone is heard continuing straight through the noise.

mechanismEn.name: The auditory system infers that the tone continued and was merely masked, because that is overwhelmingly the likelier state of the world

entries.notesEn: The auditory equivalent of blind-spot filling-in, and the reason conversation survives a passing lorry.

impl.notes: A tone with a gap and a noise burst that can be switched on and off independently.
