Gap with silence, gap with noise, gap with quiet noise — three states, one control, and the whole phenomenon is audible in ten seconds. Add the phonemic-restoration version with our own recorded sentence.

first.where: Beiträge zur Analyse der Gesichtswahrnehmungen, Erste Abhandlung. Zeitschrift für Psychologie und Physiologie der Sinnesorgane 23: 1–32

entries.effectEn: Edges are seen where there is no luminance or colour change at all.

mechanismEn.name: Boundary completion in early visual cortex, driven by aligned terminations and occlusion cues

entries.notesEn: Catalogued as an umbrella entry; the individual figures have their own rows.

impl.notes: An umbrella exhibit rather than a single demo: Schumann figure, Kanizsa triangle, Ehrenstein, Varin and abutting gratings on one page with shared controls, so the visitor can see they are one family.

first.where: Invented for the lithograph Belvedere, first printed May 1958

entries.effectEn: A wireframe cube whose edges cross in a way no cube can.

mechanismEn.name: Occlusion cues at two edge crossings are set in contradiction; each is accepted locally

entries.notesEn: The boy in Belvedere is holding one, while sitting on a bench in front of a building that makes the same mistake at architectural scale.

impl.notes: The physical trick works: build a cube with two edges genuinely broken and offset in depth, photograph or render from the right angle. The orbit reveal is the exhibit.

first.by: Lionel S. Penrose and Roger Penrose (the class, and the name)
first.where: Impossible objects: a special type of visual illusion. British Journal of Psychology 49(1): 31–33

entries.effectEn: A flat drawing immediately and involuntarily read as a solid object that cannot exist.

mechanismEn.name: Local-to-global inconsistency: the visual system builds a 3D interpretation from local junctions and never checks that they can all hold at once

entries.notesEn: Hogarth Satire on False Perspective (1754) is arguably the first deliberate impossible picture, and it is public domain — worth showing.

impl.notes: Umbrella exhibit with a shared orbit control across tribar, staircase, cube and blivet. One mechanism, four costumes.

first.by: Arien Mack and Irvin Rock coined the term; Simons and Chabris (1999) produced the famous demonstration
first.where: Mack and Rock, Inattentional Blindness, MIT Press, 1998 (term 1992); Simons and Chabris, Gorillas in our midst. Perception 28(9): 1059–1074, 1999

entries.effectEn: Asked to count basketball passes, about half of observers fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the middle of the scene.

mechanismEn.name: Without attention there is very little perception of unexpected objects, however salient they are physically

entries.notesEn: The single hardest entry in the catalogue to present honestly, because the demonstration is destroyed by its own title.

impl.notes: Only works once per visitor, and only if they do not know what is coming — so it must not be labelled. The honest approach is to film our own version with a different unexpected event, present it as a counting task at the top of the attention section, and reveal afterwards. Anyone who has seen the gorilla video is immune, so ask first and branch.

first.where: Minnaert 1954; Lynch and Livingston 2001

entries.effectEn: The pool of water on a hot road that is never there — an inverted image of the sky, displaced below the object.

mechanismEn.name: A steep temperature gradient just above hot ground bends light upward into the eye, producing an inverted image below the true one

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.by: Patrick Haggard, Sam Clark and Jeri Kalogeras
first.where: Voluntary action and conscious awareness. Nature Neuroscience 5(4): 382–385

entries.effectEn: When you cause something, your action feels later than it was and its consequence feels earlier — the two are pulled together in time. When the same movement is produced involuntarily, they are pushed apart.

mechanismEn.name: Time perception is warped by the sense of agency, which makes the binding a measurable index of whether an action felt like yours

entries.notesEn: Bridges the agency and time sections: a distortion of felt time that is caused by a sense of authorship.

impl.notes: A Libet clock, a keypress, a tone, and a judgement of when each happened. Runs in a browser and produces the visitor own binding in milliseconds. Frame timing must be measured rather than assumed; that caveat belongs on the page.

first.by: Galileo Galilei (description); Hermann von Helmholtz (1867, the name)
first.where: Galilei, Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo, 1632; Helmholtz, Handbuch der physiologischen Optik, 1867

entries.effectEn: A light patch on a dark ground looks larger than an equally sized dark patch on a light ground.

mechanismEn.name: Optical scatter and the non-linear response of receptors spread the bright region beyond its physical border

entries.notesEn: The reason a waxing crescent moon looks like it belongs to a larger sphere than the earthshine disc behind it.

impl.notes: Paired squares with a luminance slider; at low display brightness the effect nearly vanishes, which is itself worth showing.

first.where: Studies from the Laboratory of Experimental Psychology of the University of Wisconsin. II. American Journal of Psychology 4(3): 381–428

entries.effectEn: Two identical ring segments stacked one above the other look different in size; the lower looks distinctly larger.

mechanismEn.name: Local comparison of the adjacent short and long edges rather than of the whole figures

entries.notesEn: Sold for a century as a toy: two identical curved train-track pieces that never look identical.

impl.notes: Two SVG ring segments generated from one set of parameters, draggable so the visitor can slide one over the other and watch them coincide. The drag is the whole demonstration.

first.where: Margini quasi-percettivi in campi con stimolazione omogenea. Rivista di Psicologia 49(1): 7–30

entries.effectEn: Three notched discs produce a bright white triangle with crisp edges that exists nowhere in the image.

mechanismEn.name: Contour completion behind an inferred occluder; the triangle is seen as nearer and brighter than the page
Cells in V1 and V2 respond to illusory contours as if they were real

entries.notesEn: The most reproduced illusion in psychology textbooks, and one of the cheapest to build well.

impl.notes: Three pac-men whose notch rotation is on a slider; at a certain misalignment the triangle disappears entirely. Add a brightness probe showing the illusory interior is the same value as the page.

first.by: John Cohen, C. E. M. Hansel and John D. Sylvester
first.where: A new phenomenon in time judgment. Nature 172(4385): 901

entries.effectEn: Stimuli separated by equal time intervals seem unequally spaced in time if the spatial gaps between them differ. Longer distance, longer felt interval.

mechanismEn.name: A prior for constant speed: if the gap was longer, more time must have passed

entries.notesEn: Kappa and tau together make the argument that space and time are not judged independently.

impl.notes: Three flashes at adjustable positions with fixed timing; the visitor judges whether the intervals were equal. Pairs with the tau effect in one exhibit, since they are one prior seen twice.

first.by: Hans Wallach and Donald N. O Connell
first.where: The kinetic depth effect. Journal of Experimental Psychology 45(4): 205–217

entries.effectEn: The shadow of a bent wire is a meaningless flat tangle until it rotates, at which point its three-dimensional shape is immediate and unmistakable.

mechanismEn.name: Structure recovered from the pattern of relative velocities under the assumption of rigidity

entries.notesEn: Also the basis of the spinning dancer, catalogued under ambiguous figures.

impl.notes: A random-dot cylinder projected orthographically: stop it and it is a flat cloud, start it and it is a cylinder — with an ambiguous rotation direction that flips, which is a bonus bistability demo.

first.where: Principles of Gestalt Psychology. Harcourt, Brace and Company, 1935

entries.effectEn: A uniform grey ring spanning a light and a dark background looks uniform — until it is split, at which point the two halves separate dramatically in lightness.

mechanismEn.name: Grouping decides the frame of reference: one object takes one lightness, two objects take two

entries.notesEn: One of the few illusions where an animation is strictly better than the printed figure, because the transition is the phenomenon.

impl.notes: A slider that separates the two ring halves continuously. Watching the lightness split open as the gap grows is far better than two static images.

first.where: Demonstration einer katatonieartigen Erscheinung beim Gesunden. Neurologisches Zentralblatt 34: 290–291

entries.effectEn: Press the backs of your hands hard against a doorframe for thirty seconds, then step away. Your arms rise on their own, and it does not feel like you doing it.

mechanismEn.name: Sustained involuntary motor output persisting after the voluntary contraction ends, generated below the level at which intention is represented — which is why it feels alien
mechanismEn.by: Kohnstamm 1915; modern work by Haggard and colleagues

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from tactile/body-ownership. The category audit put it plainly: this is an involuntary movement, not a question of ownership. It is the clearest single member of the new motor-efferent category, which the audit confirmed independently of this project own proposal for an efferent cause.

impl.notes: Instructions and a timer — that is the whole build, and it works on everyone. Belongs at the top of the tactile section next to the Aristotle illusion, because both need nothing but a body.

first.where: La perception de la causalité. Publications Universitaires de Louvain, 1946; English translation 1963

entries.effectEn: A square slides into a second square, which immediately moves off. You do not infer that the first caused the second — you see it, as directly as you see the colours.

mechanismEn.name: Causation is perceived, not deduced: the impression depends on precise timing and direction, and collapses if the delay exceeds about 150 ms

entries.notesEn: Michotte also described entraining (the objects move off together) and triggering. Worth building all three.

impl.notes: Two squares and a delay slider. At zero delay it is a collision; at 200 ms it is two unrelated events; in between the visitor can watch causation drain out of the display. Among the cheapest and most philosophically loaded demos available, and nobody else builds it well.

first.by: Frederick A. A. Kingdom, Ali Yoonessi and Elena Gheorghiu (McGill University)
first.where: Leaning tower illusion: a new illusion of perspective. Perception 36(3): 475–477

entries.effectEn: Two identical photographs of a receding tower placed side by side look like two towers leaning at different angles.

mechanismEn.name: The visual system treats the pair as one scene, so two sets of parallel edges that should converge on a shared vanishing point but do not are read as different physical tilts

entries.notesEn: Cheap to build and unusually convincing, because the visitor can verify the two images are byte-identical.

impl.notes: Two copies of one photograph, with a slider for the gap between them and a toggle that flips the second copy horizontally, which kills the effect. Needs our own photograph of a receding structure rather than the usual Pisa shot.

first.where: Minnaert 1954; Lynch and Livingston 2001

entries.effectEn: A vertical shaft of light standing above a light source in freezing air, appearing to rise from the ground into the sky.

mechanismEn.name: Specular reflection from the flat faces of horizontally drifting ice crystals; the pillar is a collection of reflections, not a beam

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2005 entry; created some time before 2005

entries.effectEn: Twelve lilac discs in a ring, one blinking off at a time, produce a running green gap — and then, with steady fixation, the lilac discs vanish entirely and only the green chaser remains.

mechanismEn.name: Three effects stacked: apparent motion of the gap, a negative afterimage in the complementary colour, and Troxler fading of the peripheral discs

entries.notesEn: The best single demonstration of several mechanisms combining, which is why it earns a prominent place on the site.

impl.notes: Trivial to build and one of the most effective demos available: twelve blurred discs, one hidden at a time, a fixation cross, and a speed slider. Worth staging in three steps so the visitor notices each of the three effects separately.

first.by: Leon D. Harmon and Béla Julesz
first.where: Masking in visual recognition: effects of two-dimensional filtered noise. Science 180(4091): 1194–1197

entries.effectEn: A face reduced to coarse grey blocks is unrecognisable — until you blur it, squint, or step back, at which point it is obviously Lincoln.

mechanismEn.name: Block quantisation adds spurious high-frequency edges that mask the low-frequency face information; removing them by blurring unmasks the face

entries.notesEn: Also why pixelating a face is poor anonymisation: the information survives the quantisation and blurring brings it back.

impl.notes: Our own portrait, a block-size slider and a blur slider. Shares the filtering pipeline with hybrid-image, so it is nearly free once that exists. The counter-intuitive part — that ADDING blur helps — is the lesson.

first.where: Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psychological Review 90(4): 293–315

entries.effectEn: Given a description of Linda, most people rate bank teller and feminist as more probable than bank teller. It cannot be.

mechanismEn.name: Judgement by representativeness: the conjunction fits the description better, and fit is substituted for probability

entries.notesEn: The framing has been criticised — some of the effect is pragmatic inference about what the question means, not a failure of logic. Worth presenting both readings.

impl.notes: Ask the question before explaining anything, record the answer, then show the set diagram and the running tally of visitor responses. Asking first is the entire design.

first.where: The moon tilt illusion. Perception 27(10): 1229–1232

entries.effectEn: With the Sun and the Moon both visible, the Moon lit face does not appear to point at the Sun — the light seems to arrive from the wrong direction entirely.

mechanismEn.name: The observer expects the line from Sun to Moon to appear straight and of constant slope; under perspective projection onto the perceived sky dome a great circle appears curved

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9 and no longer a candidate for removal. The same author later became better known for kernel methods in machine learning.

impl.notes: A sky-dome simulation with a stretched string between Sun and Moon. Worth building only if the entry earns a proper citation first.

first.where: Über die Wirkung der räumlichen Vertheilung des Lichtreizes auf die Netzhaut. Sitzungsberichte der kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften 52: 303–322

entries.effectEn: Where a luminance ramp meets a flat region, a bright band appears on the light side and a dark band on the dark side. Neither is in the image.

mechanismEn.name: Lateral inhibition in the retina exaggerates the second derivative of the luminance profile
Empirical account: the percept reflects the luminance profiles that such images usually come from in natural scenes

entries.notesEn: Radiologists are taught about them, because Mach bands at the edge of a dense structure get read as fractures or caries that are not there.

impl.notes: Canvas ramp with a slider on ramp steepness and a luminance-profile plot underneath that stays visibly flat where the eye insists on a band. Masking the surround with a movable window proves the band is not in the pixels.

first.where: Coined on her website after discovering that others shared her false memory of Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s

entries.effectEn: Large numbers of people share the same specific false memory — a line of dialogue, a brand spelling, a logo detail.

mechanismEn.name: Schema-driven reconstruction plus social reinforcement: the same plausible error is generated independently by many people and then confirmed by finding others who made it

entries.notesEn: A useful bridge from laboratory false memory to something visitors already argue about online.

impl.notes: A recognition quiz over logos and quotations with confidence ratings, then the correct versions. Choose examples that work in the site three language communities rather than only American ones — the Soviet and post-Soviet material would be far more interesting to this audience.

first.where: Color adaptation of edge-detectors in the human visual system. Science 149(3688): 1115–1116

entries.effectEn: After a few minutes alternating between a red horizontal grating and a green vertical one, black-and-white gratings take on the opposite colours — and only at the matching orientation.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation of cells jointly tuned to colour and orientation, early in the cortex
Error-correction learning rather than fatigue, which would explain the extraordinary persistence

entries.notesEn: The only entry in this catalogue where the demonstration has a genuine duty of care attached. Treat the warning as part of the implementation, not decoration.

impl.notes: Timed induction with a countdown, then a test grating the visitor can rotate. The site MUST carry a clear warning before induction: Jones and Holding measured the aftereffect persisting for months after prolonged exposure. Cap the induction timer, make it opt-in, and say plainly what the risk is.

first.where: Hearing lips and seeing voices. Nature 264(5588): 746–748

entries.effectEn: Hear ba, watch a face say ga, and you perceive da. Close your eyes and it is ba again. Knowing does not help.

mechanismEn.name: Speech perception fuses acoustic and visual articulatory evidence before it reaches awareness, and the fusion is obligatory

entries.notesEn: The strongest everyday demonstration that hearing is not a sealed channel. Replication rates vary a lot across languages and individuals, which the page should mention rather than promising it will work for everyone.

impl.notes: Film our own talker — ideally in all three site languages, since the effect varies by language and that comparison would be genuinely novel. Controls: audio only, video only, both, and a close-your-eyes prompt. The eyes-closed toggle is the whole argument and must be one click.

first.by: Reynaud des Marchais recorded the West African use; miraculin isolated in 1968
first.where: Des Marchais, account of his 1725 voyage to West Africa

entries.effectEn: Chew a miracle berry and for the next half hour lemons taste like lemonade, vinegar like sweet wine.

mechanismEn.name: Miraculin binds to sweet receptors and only activates them at low pH, so acids become sweet — the taste is genuinely produced, not merely imagined

entries.notesEn: Arguably not an illusion at all but a pharmacological change to the receptor — a useful boundary case for the section on what counts.

impl.notes: Cannot be delivered by a web page. Explanation, plus the note that the tablets are sold legally in most of Europe, so a visitor who wants to try it can.

first.by: Discussed since Plato Timaeus; the modern analysis is twentieth-century
first.where: Plato, Timaeus; analysed at length by Gregory and by Gardner, The Ambidextrous Universe, 1964

entries.effectEn: A mirror reverses left and right but not up and down. It does neither: it reverses front and back, and the puzzle is entirely about what the words mean.

mechanismEn.name: Reflection inverts the axis perpendicular to the mirror. The apparent left-right asymmetry comes from the observer imagining themselves rotated about a vertical axis to face the other way

entries.notesEn: Gregory optical-paradox example. Arguably a linguistic illusion wearing an optical costume, which is itself worth saying on the page.

impl.notes: A 3D object and a mirror plane the visitor can reorient, with the reversed axis highlighted. Lay the mirror on the floor and the paradox reverses with it, which is the demonstration.

first.where: Beobachtungen über einige Bedingungen der Entstehung von Tönen. Annalen der Physik und Chemie 53: 417–436

entries.effectEn: Remove the fundamental frequency from a harmonic tone entirely and the pitch does not change.

mechanismEn.name: Pitch is derived from the periodicity of the whole harmonic pattern, not from energy at the fundamental

entries.notesEn: The reason a small phone speaker with no response below 300 Hz can still play a bass line. The bass is not there; you supply it.

impl.notes: A harmonic stack with a per-harmonic mute switch and a live spectrum. Muting the fundamental while the perceived pitch holds is the entire demonstration, and it takes one checkbox.

first.by: Paul Curry (amateur magician), reported by Martin Gardner (1956)
first.where: Gardner, Mathematics, Magic and Mystery. Dover, 1956, pp. 139–150

entries.effectEn: The same four pieces rearranged into what looks like the same triangle leave a square hole. The hypotenuse was never straight.

mechanismEn.name: The two sub-triangles have slightly different slopes, so the figure is a thin quadrilateral both times, bulging one way and then the other. The area difference is exactly one square unit

entries.notesEn: A mathematical rather than a perceptual illusion, and the site should say so: the eye is not malfunctioning, it is being asked to judge a slope difference of about one degree.

impl.notes: Draggable pieces plus a straightedge overlay along the hypotenuse and a zoom that exaggerates the vertical scale. The exaggerated view is what turns a trick into an explanation.

first.by: Used deliberately by painters since Leonardo; the physics in Minnaert
first.where: Leonardo, Trattato della pittura; Minnaert 1954

entries.effectEn: In mist, a near small object and a far large one deliver the same light, and distance becomes genuinely undecidable. Hills appear closer or further with the humidity.

mechanismEn.name: Scattering removes the contrast and colour cues that normally carry distance, leaving the image underdetermined — the ambiguity is in the light, not in the observer

entries.notesEn: Gregory canonical optical-ambiguity example. Leonardo turned it into a painting technique four centuries before anyone measured it.

first.where: On the manufacture and theory of diffraction-gratings. Philosophical Magazine 47(310): 81–93

entries.effectEn: Two overlaid periodic patterns produce a large-scale pattern present in neither.

mechanismEn.name: Spatial beat frequency between the two periods — a physical interference in the image, not a perceptual illusion

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. Belongs to physical optics rather than perception — the pattern is genuinely in the image — and the site should label it as such. Moved to physical/optics in W17: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too.

impl.notes: Two canvas layers with independent rotation and pitch. Cheap, hypnotic, and a good illustration of the physical/perceptual distinction — this one is genuinely in the image.

first.where: A problem in probability (letter). The American Statistician 29(1): 67

entries.effectEn: Three doors, one car. You pick one, the host opens a goat door, and switching wins two thirds of the time. Almost nobody believes this on first hearing.

mechanismEn.name: The host choice is not independent of where the car is, so his action carries information; intuition treats the remaining two doors as symmetric when they are not

entries.notesEn: Classified here as a cognitive illusion in Kahneman sense rather than a perceptual one, and the site should mark that boundary explicitly.

impl.notes: Playable doors plus a simulator that runs ten thousand trials of both strategies and plots the convergence. Being able to play badly and then watch the simulation is far more persuasive than the proof. Add the hundred-door variant, which makes the intuition click for most people immediately.

first.where: Minnaert 1954

entries.effectEn: The lunar counterpart of the sun dog: bright patches flanking the moon, usually colourless because the light is too faint for colour vision.

mechanismEn.name: Identical crystal optics to the sun dog; the absence of colour is the observer scotopic vision, which makes this a hybrid of an optical and a physiological cause

entries.notesEn: A useful edge case: the phenomenon is optical, its colourlessness is physiological. The two causes stack in one percept.

first.by: Aristotle and earlier; discussed by Ptolemy and by Ibn al-Haytham
first.where: Recorded across Greek, Chinese and Arabic sources; Ross and Plug (2002) trace the sequence

entries.effectEn: The Moon looks substantially larger near the horizon than high in the sky, although its angular size is unchanged and can be measured to be so.

mechanismEn.name: Apparent distance: the horizon sky reads as further away, so a constant angular size is scaled up
Relative size against terrain and objects on the horizon
Oculomotor micropsia from convergence changes when the gaze is raised

entries.notesEn: Still genuinely unresolved after two thousand years — the honest thing for the site to say. Ross and Plug count more than twenty published explanations.

impl.notes: A canvas sky with a horizon and a slider for elevation; the disc stays pixel-identical while the surroundings change. Add the classic test: view it through a tube and the illusion collapses.

first.where: Age in the development of closure ability in children. Canadian Journal of Psychology 11(4): 219–226

entries.effectEn: A face reduced to hard black-and-white blobs is meaningless noise — until you see it, after which you can never unsee it.

mechanismEn.name: Perceptual closure: once a face hypothesis is available, the same image is organised completely differently

entries.notesEn: Among the best demonstrations that perception is not reversible — knowledge permanently changes what the image looks like.

impl.notes: Generate from our own photographs with a threshold slider. The one-way door is the exhibit: record how long before the visitor reports seeing it, and note that the timer cannot be run twice on the same image.

first.by: Robert Addams; described by Aristotle and Lucretius in antiquity, and by Purkyně in 1820
first.where: An account of a peculiar optical phenomenon seen after having looked at a moving body. London and Edinburgh Philosophical Magazine 5: 373–374

entries.effectEn: After watching motion in one direction for a minute, a stationary scene drifts the other way — while staying perfectly still.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation of direction-selective neurons, unbalancing the opponent motion signal

entries.notesEn: The oldest illusion in the catalogue with an unbroken written record, and the one that established that perception has adaptable components.

impl.notes: Expanding spiral or drifting grating, timed adaptation, then a still test image with a countdown of how long the aftereffect lasts. Logging the duration turns it into data the visitor produced.

first.where: The influence of terminators on motion integration across space. Vision Research 32(2): 263–273

entries.effectEn: Line segments visible only through separated apertures are bound into one coherently moving object once the occluders are made visible.

mechanismEn.name: Line terminators at aperture edges carry spurious motion signals; making the occluders visible tells the visual system to discount them and integrate the contours into one object

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9.

impl.notes: A diamond moving behind four occluders, with an occluder-visibility toggle. Visible occluders bind the segments; invisible ones leave four unrelated lines.

first.by: Yoram S. Bonneh, Alexander Cooperman and Dov Sagi
first.where: Motion-induced blindness in normal observers. Nature 411(6839): 798–801

entries.effectEn: Bright yellow dots on a rotating field of blue crosses simply vanish, one at a time, for seconds, and come back.

mechanismEn.name: A competition between the moving pattern and the static targets, possibly a form of perceptual rivalry

entries.notesEn: Disturbing to experience, which is part of the point: a bright, high-contrast, perfectly visible object disappears from a perfectly healthy visual system.

impl.notes: Canvas with rotating cross field, three targets, a fixation point and a hold-to-report control: the visitor holds a key while a dot is missing, and the page plots their disappearance intervals. Cheap to build, and it produces a real psychophysical curve.

first.where: Optische Urteilstäuschungen. Archiv für Anatomie und Physiologie, Physiologische Abteilung, Suppl. 1889: 263–270

entries.effectEn: Two shafts of identical length look unequal when one ends in outward fins and the other in inward arrowheads.

mechanismEn.name: Misapplied size constancy — the fins read as near and far corners of a carpentered world
Centroid / centre-of-gravity: the visual system locates the shaft end at the centroid of the whole wing, not at the vertex
Low-level spatial filtering reproduces the effect without any inference about depth

entries.notesEn: Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1966) reported that susceptibility varies with how rectangular the built environment is. The claim is widely repeated and has been challenged since on sampling and analysis grounds — the site should present it as a contested classic, not a settled fact. The category audit flags Coren et al. 1976 empirical factor analysis as disagreeing with this catalogue geometric partition: it merges geometric-direction with geometric-shape and splits geometric-size into contrast and extent. That is the one place a canonical scheme actively contradicts the taxonomy used here, and it is unresolved.

impl.notes: Slider sweeps fin angle from -70 to +70 degrees while both shafts stay provably equal; a toggle drops a ruler over them. Second slider for fin length, since the effect scales with it.

first.by: Necker (the first documented case); the general phenomenon named much later
first.where: Necker 1832; the modern framing dates from the Gestalt tradition onward

entries.effectEn: One unchanging stimulus produces a sequence of spontaneous, unpredictable changes in what is perceived.

mechanismEn.name: Competition between interpretations with adaptation and noise; switch timing follows a gamma distribution across many different bistable stimuli

entries.notesEn: Also occurs in audition (Deutsch bistable stimuli) and olfaction, which the site should note as evidence that this is a general principle rather than a quirk of vision.

impl.notes: Umbrella exhibit: several bistable stimuli sharing one hold-to-report mechanism, so the visitor can compare their own switch rates across Necker cube, Rubin vase, spinning dancer and binocular rivalry. The cross-stimulus comparison is genuinely informative and nobody else does it.

first.where: Farbige Gitter, Abbildung auf der Netzhaut und übertragungstheoretische Beschreibung der Farbwahrnehmung. Dissertation, LMU München, 1970

entries.effectEn: Identical coloured spheres or stripes look like entirely different hues depending on whether the overlaid grid lines are one colour or another.

mechanismEn.name: Chromatic assimilation toward the overlaid pattern, the colour analogue of the White effect

entries.notesEn: The 2019 colour-assimilation grid (a grey photograph with coloured grid lines that looks fully coloured) is the same mechanism and went viral on its own; catalogued here as a variant.

impl.notes: Canvas with a colour picker and an eyedropper the visitor can drop on any pixel to read its true RGB. The eyedropper is essential: without a measurement, this illusion is just an assertion. A second mode implements the Kolås grid over a genuinely greyscale photograph.

first.where: Pseudoptics, Milton Bradley, 1894; restated as Die verschobene Schachbrettfigur, Zeitschrift für Psychologie 15: 184–188, 1897

entries.effectEn: The high-contrast ancestor of the café wall: offset chequer rows without grey mortar, already visibly wedged.

mechanismEn.name: Same border-locking mechanism, weaker without intermediate-luminance mortar

entries.notesEn: Kept as its own entry because the priority question only makes sense if the earlier figure has a name.

impl.notes: A preset of the café-wall renderer with mortar width zero. Keeping it as a separate catalogue entry preserves the history; the site can show it inside the café-wall exhibit.

first.by: William Ely Hill; a German postcard version dates from 1888
first.where: Puck, 6 November 1915

entries.effectEn: A young woman turned away, or an old woman in profile. The young woman ear is the old woman eye; her chin is the nose.

mechanismEn.name: Two object hypotheses competing over the same contours, with the same feature serving different roles in each

entries.notesEn: Nicholls et al. 2018 found an own-age bias: younger observers see the young woman first, older observers the old woman.

impl.notes: Public domain. Worth adding an overlay that traces each reading on demand, since a significant fraction of viewers never find the second one unaided.

first.where: Observations on some remarkable optical phaenomena seen in Switzerland. London and Edinburgh Philosophical Magazine 1(5): 329–337

entries.effectEn: A wireframe cube flips between two depth interpretations, spontaneously and beyond voluntary control.

mechanismEn.name: Two equally good 3D interpretations of one 2D projection; perception alternates because neither wins, with adaptation driving the switches

entries.notesEn: Switch rate is remarkably stable within a person and varies a lot between people, which makes it a genuinely good self-measurement exhibit.

impl.notes: Cube plus a hold-to-report control that logs each flip, so the page can show the visitor their own switch-rate distribution. That is a real measurement and it is two hours of work. Add shading and occlusion toggles that disambiguate it, which kill the flipping entirely.

first.by: Described across the early physiological literature; Purkyně gives an extended treatment
first.where: Purkyně, Neue Beiträge zur Kenntniss des Sehens in subjectiver Hinsicht, 1825

entries.effectEn: After fixating a coloured patch, looking at a blank field produces a patch of the complementary colour.

mechanismEn.name: Photoreceptor and opponent-channel adaptation
A cortical contribution as well — afterimage colour can be modulated by the contours it fills

impl.notes: Fixation cross, timed coloured field, then white. Add the van Lier variant, where the afterimage colour depends on which outline is shown afterwards — that is the interesting part and it is barely harder to build.

first.where: Fenomeni di contrasto e diffusione cromatica nell organizzazione spaziale del campo percettivo. Rivista di Psicologia 65: 101–128

entries.effectEn: Coloured line segments set inside a black grid make the colour appear to glow and spread through an illusory transparent disc that is not drawn.

mechanismEn.name: Colour spreading confined by illusory contours; depends on luminance contrast between the coloured and black segments
Perceived transparency: the disc is seen as a coloured veil lying over the grid

entries.notesEn: Pairs with the watercolour illusion and the Ehrenstein figure as three routes to the same conclusion: colour is assigned to regions, not pixels.

impl.notes: Grid plus inner cross with a luminance slider on the coloured segments. The effect has a narrow luminance window and collapses outside it, which the visitor should be able to find.

first.by: Gerrit de Veer, on the Barents expedition
first.where: De Veer, journal of the 1596–1597 wintering on Novaya Zemlya

entries.effectEn: The sun seen rising two weeks before it geometrically can. De Veer crew were disbelieved for three centuries.

mechanismEn.name: Light ducted through an inversion layer follows the curvature of the earth, so an object below the horizon is seen above it

entries.notesEn: Gregory optical-paradox cell: the percept contradicts what is geometrically possible, and the cause is entirely in the light.

first.where: A visual sense of number. Current Biology 18(6): 425–428

entries.effectEn: After staring at a dense field of dots, a following field of medium density looks much sparser than the same field does after adapting to a sparse one.

mechanismEn.name: A dedicated sense of numerosity that adapts like colour or motion
Texture-density adaptation rather than number as such

entries.notesEn: The interpretation is contested — whether it is number or density that adapts is an open argument, and the demo should say so.

impl.notes: Two adapting patches left and right, then matched test patches. Needs a timed sequence and a forced-choice response to make the effect legible to the visitor.

first.where: An auditory illusion. Nature 251(5473): 307–309

entries.effectEn: Two tones an octave apart alternate between the ears. Most listeners hear a single tone hopping from ear to ear while its pitch alternates high and low — and right-handers usually hear the high tone on the right regardless of where it actually is.

mechanismEn.name: Pitch is taken from one ear and location from the other; which ear wins depends on handedness and therefore on hemispheric organisation

entries.notesEn: One of the few perceptual illusions whose outcome depends on handedness, which is why it ended up in the neuropsychology literature rather than only in psychoacoustics.

impl.notes: Headphones mandatory, with a channel check before it plays — on speakers this is simply a different stimulus and the illusion does not exist. Add a swap-channels button: most listeners report no change, which is the striking part. Ask about handedness and show the aggregate.

first.where: The oculogravic illusion. AMA Archives of Ophthalmology 48(5): 605–615

entries.effectEn: Under sustained linear acceleration, a fixed visual target appears to rise or tilt — the visual counterpart of the somatogravic illusion.

mechanismEn.name: The apparent vertical is set by the resultant of gravity and acceleration, and visual space is referred to that apparent vertical

impl.notes: Shares the vector diagram with the somatogravic illusion.

first.by: Ashton Graybiel and Dean I. Hupp
first.where: The oculogyral illusion. Journal of Aviation Medicine 17: 3–27

entries.effectEn: In the dark, a target fixed to a rotating chair appears to move and shift position relative to the observer during angular acceleration.

mechanismEn.name: Vestibular signals about self-rotation are combined with retinal position to compute target motion, and when the vestibular signal is wrong so is the result

impl.notes: Needs a rotating chair in a dark room. Explanation only.

first.by: Peter U. Tse, James Intriligator, Josée Rivest and Patrick Cavanagh
first.where: Attention and the subjective expansion of time. Perception & Psychophysics 66(7): 1171–1189

entries.effectEn: In a stream of identical stimuli, an odd one out is judged to have lasted longer — although every item has the same duration.

mechanismEn.name: Attention increases the rate of processing, and more processing is read as more time

entries.notesEn: The likely basis of the everyday report that time slows down in an accident — and the reason that report is probably about memory rather than about experience.

impl.notes: A stream of repeated shapes with one oddball, and a duration-matching task afterwards. Produces the visitor own overestimate as a number.

first.by: Rachel S. Herz and Julia von Clef
first.where: The influence of verbal labeling on the perception of odors: evidence for olfactory illusions? Perception 30(3): 381–391

entries.effectEn: One bottle, two labels. Called parmesan the smell is pleasant; called vomit the identical molecule is disgusting — and the change is in the experience, not just the rating.

mechanismEn.name: Smell has almost no independent perceptual vocabulary, so the label supplies the interpretation and the interpretation shapes the percept

entries.notesEn: The strongest published case that there are olfactory illusions at all — a question the field argued about for years, since smell has so few of them compared with vision.

impl.notes: Cannot be delivered through a screen. A do-it-yourself protocol with two friends and one bottle, plus the honest note that the effect needs a genuinely ambiguous odour to work.

first.by: Term coined in 1964; the movement defined by the MoMA exhibition The Responsive Eye (1965)
first.where: Seitz, The Responsive Eye, Museum of Modern Art, 1965

entries.effectEn: Paintings built specifically to make a static surface shimmer, pulse, warp or move.

mechanismEn.name: Deliberate exploitation of the same mechanisms catalogued elsewhere here: orientation contrast, lateral inhibition, illusory motion from high-contrast periodic patterns, moiré

entries.notesEn: The section where the site must be most careful about rights, and where building rather than copying is both legally and pedagogically better.

impl.notes: Everything from this period is in copyright. Build generative op-art in the same idioms — high-contrast periodic fields with controllable frequency, phase and warp — and credit the tradition without reproducing the works. A generative approach is also more honest about what the effects depend on.

first.where: Über geometrisch-optische Täuschungen. Jahresbericht des Physikalischen Vereins zu Frankfurt am Main 1854–1855: 37–47

entries.effectEn: A stretch of space divided by tick marks looks longer than an equal empty stretch beside it.

mechanismEn.name: The number of elements inside an extent inflates the judged extent

entries.notesEn: Historically the important one: Oppel 1855 is the paper that names the whole field of geometrical-optical illusions, and it is available in English translation since 2017.

impl.notes: Slider on tick count from 0 to 40; the filled half visibly grows while the measured length does not.

first.where: Shape as a function of the vector-field. The American Journal of Psychology 52(1): 31–45

entries.effectEn: A square or circle drawn over a radial or concentric background is distorted out of shape.

mechanismEn.name: Orbison own vector-field account: the background imposes a field of directional forces that the figure is judged within

entries.notesEn: A superset of Hering and Wundt rather than a separate mechanism, which is the usual modern reading.

impl.notes: Background selector (radial fan, concentric rings, hyperbolic) times figure selector (square, circle, hexagon). A kinetic version, where the background rotates slowly, is markedly stronger.

first.where: Japanese Optical and Geometrical Art. Dover Publications, 1977

entries.effectEn: An inset of horizontally oriented checks inside a field of vertical ones appears to float and slide independently at the slightest movement of the page or the eye.

mechanismEn.name: The two textures give different aperture-problem solutions, so their motion signals fail to integrate into one surface

entries.notesEn: A rare case where the catalogue can name the exact moment an illusion crossed from design into science.

impl.notes: Procedural check field with sliders on check aspect ratio and inset size, plus a gentle programmatic jitter so the effect appears without the visitor having to shake their screen.

first.by: Macdonald Critchley coined the term; established as a clinical entity by Bender, Feldman and Sobin (1968)
first.where: Bender, Feldman and Sobin, Palinopsia. Brain 91(2): 321–338, 1968

entries.effectEn: An image persists or recurs after the object has gone — sometimes for minutes, sometimes reappearing hours later, sometimes trailing behind moving objects.

mechanismEn.name: Pathological afterimage, distinct from the normal physiological one; associated with occipital lesions, seizures and some drugs

impl.notes: Explanation only, cross-linked to the normal afterimage entries so the boundary between physiological and pathological is explicit.

first.where: Parchment-skin illusion: sound-biased touch. Current Biology 8(6): R190

entries.effectEn: Rub your palms together while hearing the rubbing sound played back with the high frequencies boosted, and your skin feels dry and papery.

mechanismEn.name: Texture is judged from a combination of touch and the sound the touch makes; alter the sound and the felt texture follows

entries.notesEn: Also the reason a crisp packet sounds fresher when the crunch is louder — the same group later showed the effect on food texture.

impl.notes: Genuinely doable in a browser: capture the microphone, filter it, feed it back through headphones with low latency, and ask the visitor to rub their hands. Needs microphone permission and careful latency handling, and must be clearly opt-in. A strong candidate precisely because almost nobody has built it on the web.

first.by: Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum coined the term
first.where: Die Sinnesdelirien. Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Psychiatrie 23: 1–86

entries.effectEn: Faces and objects appear in clouds, wood grain, electrical sockets and the surface of Mars.

mechanismEn.name: A face-detection system tuned for very low miss rates, which necessarily produces false alarms; face-selective cortex responds to pareidolic faces as to real ones

entries.notesEn: The Face on Mars (Viking 1, 1976) is public domain and comes with its 1998 high-resolution follow-up, which makes the pair an ideal exhibit.

impl.notes: Curated gallery plus a generator: procedural noise the visitor can reroll until a face appears, with a counter of how many rerolls it took. That makes the false-alarm rate tangible instead of anecdotal.

first.by: Oscar Reutersvärd; independently Lionel and Roger Penrose (1958)
first.where: Penrose and Penrose, Impossible objects. British Journal of Psychology 49(1): 31–33, 1958

entries.effectEn: A flight of stairs that climbs continuously through four right angles and arrives back where it started.

mechanismEn.name: Local depth relations at each step are consistent; the accumulated height around the loop is not, and the visual system never sums it

entries.notesEn: Escher Ascending and Descending (March 1960) came directly from the Penrose paper.

impl.notes: Two builds worth having: the disconnected-geometry version that reveals its gap on orbit, and the Monument Valley approach, where camera-aligned geometry lets a walker actually traverse the loop. The second is more work and far more memorable.

first.by: Oscar Reutersvärd; independently by Lionel and Roger Penrose (1958)
first.where: Reutersvärd, Opus 1, 1934 (unpublished drawing); Penrose and Penrose, Impossible objects: a special type of visual illusion. British Journal of Psychology 49(1): 31–33, 1958

entries.effectEn: Three beams meeting at right angles in a closed loop. Every corner is locally consistent; the whole cannot exist.

mechanismEn.name: The visual system interprets junctions locally and has no global consistency check, so it accepts a figure whose parts cannot be assembled
Formally: a non-trivial cohomology class on the figure — Roger Penrose wrote this up in 1992

entries.notesEn: Escher saw the Penrose paper and built Waterfall from three tribars. There are physical sculptures in Perth and Ophoven that work from one viewpoint.

impl.notes: Build the real disconnected 3D object that projects to the tribar from exactly one angle, then let the visitor orbit away from it. This is the whole point and it is only possible in 3D — the figure does not become a lie until you move.

first.by: Henry Dircks (patent, 1858); John Henry Pepper (practical version, 24 December 1862)
first.where: Dircks, The Ghost, as Produced in the Spectre Drama, 1863; Pepper demonstration at the Royal Polytechnic, London

entries.effectEn: A hidden brightly lit figure reflected in an angled sheet of glass appears as a transparent ghost standing on stage among solid actors.

mechanismEn.name: Partial reflection from a large glass sheet superimposes a virtual image on the real scene; controlling relative illumination controls the ghost opacity

entries.notesEn: Still in use: modern concert holograms are the same trick with a projection screen.

impl.notes: WebGL stage with a movable glass plane and two lighting sliders, plus a top-down schematic. The schematic is what makes it click.

first.by: Jocelyn Faubert and Andrew M. Herbert
first.where: The peripheral drift illusion: a motion illusion in the visual periphery. Perception 28(5): 617–621

entries.effectEn: A stationary sawtooth luminance pattern drifts when viewed off-centre and stops when looked at directly.

mechanismEn.name: Temporal differences in how fast high- and low-luminance regions are processed generate a false motion signal

impl.notes: Shares the renderer with rotating-snakes; presented as the parent phenomenon.

first.by: Silas Weir Mitchell coined the term; Ambroise Paré described it in the sixteenth century
first.where: Mitchell, Phantom limbs. Lippincott Magazine 8: 563–569, 1871

entries.effectEn: An amputated limb continues to be felt — its position, its movement, and very often its pain.

mechanismEn.name: The body model persists without its input; cortical reorganisation and conflicting motor predictions maintain the percept

entries.notesEn: Included because it is the strongest evidence that the body model is generated rather than received, and because the mirror box is one of the few cases where illusion research produced a treatment.

impl.notes: Not a demonstration and must never be framed as one — this is a clinical condition affecting most amputees. Explanation only, with the mirror-box therapy that came out of the research, and written with care.

first.where: Published on the CD Phantom Words and Other Curiosities, Philomel Records, 2003; discussed at length in Deutsch (2019)

entries.effectEn: Two meaningless syllables looped out of phase between the speakers, and listeners hear clear words and phrases — different ones for each listener, often reflecting what is on their mind.

mechanismEn.name: With ambiguous input the speech system imposes the most available interpretation, drawing on expectation, vocabulary and current concerns

entries.notesEn: Closely related to the electronic voice phenomenon, which is the same mechanism with a supernatural interpretation attached. Worth saying so.

impl.notes: Our own syllable pairs, offset between channels, ideally in all three site languages. Collect what visitors report hearing and show the distribution — that is the whole point and it needs no personal data.

first.where: Experimentelle Studien über das Sehen von Bewegung. Zeitschrift für Psychologie 61: 161–265

entries.effectEn: At high alternation rates between two flashed shapes, motion is seen with no object moving — a bare sense of something passing.

mechanismEn.name: Motion is computed separately from object identity; phi is what the motion system reports when the identity system has nothing to offer

entries.notesEn: Constantly confused with beta movement in popular accounts, including the claim that cinema depends on phi. It depends on beta. Worth correcting on the page.

impl.notes: One demo with an interstimulus-interval slider spanning the whole range: at long intervals two separate flashes, at medium beta movement (an object travelling), at short pure phi. Naming each regime as the visitor crosses into it is the lesson.

first.by: Baingio Pinna and Gavin J. Brelstaff
first.where: A new visual illusion of relative motion. Vision Research 40(16): 2091–2096

entries.effectEn: Two concentric rings of tilted micro-patterns counter-rotate when you move your head toward and away from the screen.

mechanismEn.name: Oblique local motion signals from the micro-patterns integrate into a rotation that is not there; initiated in area MST rather than MT

entries.notesEn: Unusual in requiring observer motion rather than stimulus motion, which makes it awkward on a phone and excellent on a desktop.

impl.notes: Procedural rings of tilted squares plus a programmatic zoom, so the effect works without asking the visitor to move. A toggle switching between zoom and head-motion instructions lets them compare.

first.where: Some proprioceptive influences on the perceptual representation of body shape and orientation. Brain 111(2): 281–297

entries.effectEn: Blindfolded, holding your nose, with a vibrator on the biceps tendon: the arm feels like it is extending, and since the finger is still on the nose, the nose grows. Participants report up to 30 cm.

mechanismEn.name: Tendon vibration excites muscle spindles, signalling a stretch that is not happening; the brain resolves the conflict by deforming the body model rather than doubting the touch

entries.notesEn: The most vivid evidence that the body model is a construction that can be edited from outside. Refiled in W17 from tactile/body-ownership: the mechanism is tendon vibration acting on the sense of limb position, which is proprioception, not body ownership.

impl.notes: Needs a vibrator at roughly 70–100 Hz on the tendon. A do-it-yourself protocol is feasible with a cheap massager; a filmed demonstration is the realistic deliverable.

first.where: Circularity in judgments of relative pitch. JASA 36(12): 2346–2353

entries.effectEn: Pitch judgements go round in a circle: each tone is heard as higher than the last, and after twelve steps you are back where you started.

mechanismEn.name: Pitch has two dimensions, chroma and height; manipulate them independently and transitivity breaks

impl.notes: Present as a pairwise comparison task: play two tones, ask which is higher, repeat twelve times, then show the visitor that their own answers form a loop. Turning it into their own contradiction is far stronger than asserting it.

first.where: Noticed in the figure Zöllner submitted to Annalen der Physik und Chemie 186(7): 500–525, which Poggendorff edited

entries.effectEn: A straight line interrupted by a wide band appears to be misaligned on the far side.

mechanismEn.name: Acute-angle expansion at the intersections with the band edges
Depth processing of the occluding band

entries.notesEn: The effect survives when the band is empty, which undercuts the purely occlusion-based accounts.

impl.notes: Drag the right-hand segment until it looks aligned, then reveal the true line. Recording the visitor error in pixels turns the demo into a measurement.

first.where: Rapports entre quelques illusions visuelles de contraste angulaire et l appréciation de grandeur des astres à l horizon. Archives Italiennes de Biologie 58: 327–329

entries.effectEn: Two identical horizontal bars placed across converging lines look unequal; the one nearer the convergence looks longer.

mechanismEn.name: Converging lines are read as linear perspective, so the upper bar is taken as further away and therefore larger

entries.notesEn: Ponzo himself proposed it as an account of the moon illusion, which is why the 1912 title is about heavenly bodies at the horizon.

impl.notes: Two bars on converging rails; slider changes convergence angle from parallel to steep, and a photo-background toggle swaps the bare lines for a real receding corridor to show the effect getting stronger.

first.by: Hans Wallach, Edwin B. Newman and Mark R. Rosenzweig; independently Helmut Haas
first.where: The precedence effect in sound localization. AJP 62(3): 315–336; Haas, doctoral thesis, Göttingen, 1949

entries.effectEn: The same sound arriving from two directions a few milliseconds apart is heard as one sound, located entirely at whichever arrived first — even when the later one is up to 10 dB louder.

mechanismEn.name: Suppression of later-arriving localisation cues, which is what makes hearing work at all in a reverberant room

entries.notesEn: The reason a public-address system with delayed rear speakers still sounds like it comes from the stage. Arguably the most commercially applied illusion in the catalogue.

impl.notes: Headphones. Two copies of a click train with an interaural delay slider from 0 to 50 ms and an independent level control on the lagging copy. Sweeping the delay past the echo threshold — where one sound becomes two — is the demonstration.

first.by: Anatole Lécuyer, Sabine Coquillart, Abderrahmane Kheddar, Paul Richard and Philippe Coiffet
first.where: Pseudo-haptic feedback: can isometric input devices simulate force feedback? Proceedings of IEEE Virtual Reality 2000: 83–90

entries.effectEn: Slow the cursor down as it crosses a region of the screen and the mouse feels heavier, or the surface feels rough. No force is applied to the hand at all.

mechanismEn.name: The brain infers force from the mismatch between motor command and visual result; changing the control-display ratio manufactures that mismatch

entries.notesEn: A whole literature of illusions invented deliberately for interfaces, invisible to every perception index the project consulted.

impl.notes: One of the best browser demos in the whole catalogue and almost nobody has built it: a draggable object whose cursor gain varies across regions. Bumps, weight, friction and stickiness, from a mouse that does nothing. Trackpads work; touchscreens are weaker.

first.where: Die Stereoskopie im Dienste der isochromen und heterochromen Photometrie. Die Naturwissenschaften 10, six-part series

entries.effectEn: A pendulum swinging in a plane appears to travel in an ellipse when one eye is covered by a dark filter.

mechanismEn.name: The darker eye signal arrives later; combining a delayed image with a current one produces a real binocular disparity, so the depth is genuinely computed, not imagined

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/motion. The effect requires two eyes with unequal latency; it is a binocular phenomenon that happens to involve motion.

impl.notes: A swinging pendulum with instructions to hold a sunglass lens over one eye. Rare case where the demo needs a physical prop; say so plainly and suggest substitutes. A software analogue that delays one eye channel needs stereo hardware and is not worth building.

first.where: Neue Beiträge zur Kenntniss des Sehens in subjectiver Hinsicht. Reimer, Berlin, 1825, pp. 109–110

entries.effectEn: As light fades, reds darken faster than blues, and the peak of visual sensitivity shifts toward the short wavelengths.

mechanismEn.name: The handover from cone vision (peak near 555 nm) to rod vision (peak near 507 nm)

entries.notesEn: Why submarine and cockpit instrument lighting is red: it preserves rod dark-adaptation.

impl.notes: Hard to do honestly on a bright screen. A dimmable scene plus the two luminosity curves plotted together is more useful than a fake, and the page should invite the visitor to test it at dusk instead.

first.by: René Descartes gave the first correct geometry; Theodoric of Freiberg had it around 1304
first.where: Les Météores, 1637

entries.effectEn: A coloured arc that has no location. It is not an object and not at a distance; every observer sees a different rainbow, made of different drops, and you cannot walk to it.

mechanismEn.name: Refraction, one internal reflection and dispersion in spherical drops, concentrating light at 42 degrees from the antisolar point

entries.notesEn: Gregory canonical example of a fiction with an optical cause. Worth the site making the point explicitly: the rainbow is real, photographable, and still not a thing in the world.

impl.notes: Ray-trace a single drop with a wavelength slider and show the 42-degree caustic forming. The valuable part for a visitor is that the rainbow has no position — moving the observer moves the rainbow.

first.where: Binocular depth perception of computer-generated patterns. Bell System Technical Journal 39(5): 1125–1162

entries.effectEn: Two fields of random dots, identical except that a region is shifted in one of them, contain no visible form at all — until viewed stereoscopically, when the region floats in depth.

mechanismEn.name: Stereopsis operates on raw binocular disparity before any form is recognised — the decisive result of twentieth-century depth research

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/depth-3d.

impl.notes: Trivially generated in canvas. Provide side-by-side pairs with a separation slider for free-fusing, and an anaglyph mode for red-cyan glasses. A control that shows the shifted region outlined proves there is genuinely nothing monocular to see.

first.by: Sharif Razzaque, Zachariah Kohn and Mary C. Whitton
first.where: Redirected walking. Eurographics 2001, Short Presentations

entries.effectEn: In VR, the world is rotated a fraction of a degree per step, below the threshold of detection. The walker believes they crossed a field in a straight line; they walked in circles in a small room.

mechanismEn.name: Vision dominates the estimate of self-motion direction, so a visual rotation slow enough to stay below threshold is absorbed rather than noticed

entries.notesEn: An illusion engineered to solve a problem rather than discovered in a laboratory, which is a category the catalogue previously had no room for.

impl.notes: Needs a headset and a room. Explanation with a diagram of the real path against the virtual one — the discrepancy between the two is the exhibit.

first.by: Recorded by the Greek sceptics as an argument about the reliability of the senses
first.where: Sextus Empiricus reports it among the tropes; Ptolemy Optics measures it

entries.effectEn: A straight stick pushed into water appears bent at the surface, and the submerged part appears both shortened and raised.

mechanismEn.name: Refraction at the water-air interface. Snell law, and the oldest illusion in philosophy

entries.notesEn: The canonical philosophical illusion, and the reason this category matters: the eye is not malfunctioning, the light really does arrive from that direction.

impl.notes: A ray diagram with a draggable viewing angle and a refractive-index slider, alongside a photograph. The point to make: this is the illusion the sceptics used to argue the senses cannot be trusted, and it is the one case where the senses are reporting the light correctly.

first.by: Jennifer J. Freyd and Ronald A. Finke
first.where: Representational momentum. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 10(1): 126–132

entries.effectEn: The final position of a moving object is remembered as further along its path than it actually was.

mechanismEn.name: The perceptual representation carries forward along the implied trajectory, as if it had inertia

entries.notesEn: Closely related to the flash-lag effect and to the same argument about prediction versus postdiction.

impl.notes: A moving object that vanishes; the visitor clicks where it stopped. The systematic forward error is measurable in pixels within a dozen trials.

first.where: Phi movement as a subtraction process. Vision Research 10(12): 1411–1430

entries.effectEn: Invert the contrast of each successive frame and the motion is seen going backwards.

mechanismEn.name: Low-level motion detectors correlate luminance across space and time; inverting contrast inverts the correlation and therefore the reported direction

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. The clearest proof that motion is computed before objects are identified.

impl.notes: A drifting pattern with a contrast-inversion toggle per frame. The reversal is immediate and unmistakable, and it is the clearest proof that motion is computed before objects are identified.

first.where: Sticking-Out Room, Institute of Contemporary Arts, London, 1964; Hughes coined the term reverspective

entries.effectEn: A relief painted so that the parts nearest the viewer carry the most distant scene. The whole work appears to swing and follow as you walk past it.

mechanismEn.name: Painted perspective overrides real depth, so the physical relief is perceived inverted — and any real parallax from viewer movement is then interpreted as object rotation
mechanismEn.by: Hughes; analysed by Wade and Hughes

entries.notesEn: One of the few illusions that is genuinely better as a physical object than as any screen version. Say so.

impl.notes: WebGL relief with painted reverse perspective and a camera that tracks the pointer to supply the parallax. Getting the painted texture right is the hard part; the geometry is trivial.

first.where: Pitch control and pitch paradoxes demonstrated with computer-synthesized sounds. JASA 46(1A Suppl.): 88

entries.effectEn: A continuously sliding tone that descends forever without arriving anywhere.

mechanismEn.name: Same octave-spaced components under a fixed envelope, but sliding continuously rather than stepping

entries.notesEn: Risset was at Bell Labs with Shepard and went on to invent much of what computer music sounds like.

impl.notes: Shares the oscillator bank with the Shepard tone; the difference is a continuous frequency ramp rather than quantised steps. One codebase, two exhibits.

first.where: Pitch and rhythm paradoxes. JASA 80(3): 961–962

entries.effectEn: A beat that speeds up forever, or slows down forever, and never arrives anywhere.

mechanismEn.name: Layers at octave-related tempi fading in and out under a fixed loudness envelope, so tempo chroma moves while overall tempo does not

entries.notesEn: Used in Shepard-tone form by electronic musicians for decades; the drop that never lands.

impl.notes: Works on speakers, which makes it one of the friendlier audio exhibits. Needs sample-accurate scheduling — schedule ahead with AudioContext.currentTime rather than driving it from setInterval, or the illusion falls apart on a busy page.

first.where: Explanation of an optical deception in the appearance of the spokes of a wheel seen through vertical apertures. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 115: 131–140

entries.effectEn: A cartwheel seen through the vertical palings of a fence has spokes that appear curved, and the curvature reverses on either side of the axle.

mechanismEn.name: Spatial sampling by the gaps combined with temporal integration: each glimpse catches the spoke at a different phase, and the sequence is read as a single bent spoke

entries.notesEn: Its rediscovery in W12 is the clearest single piece of evidence that the first pass did not exhaust its own sources: an 1825 Royal Society paper by a household name, sitting unread in a harvest the project had already made.

impl.notes: A rotating wheel behind a slatted mask, with sliders on slat width, slat spacing and rotation rate. Cheap, and it belongs at the head of the motion section as the historical ancestor of the whole stroboscopic family.

first.by: Ryan E. B. Mruczek and Gideon P. Caplovitz
first.where: The Rotating Circles Illusion, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2019 (third prize)

entries.effectEn: Circles travelling on straight paths are seen to rotate around one another.

mechanismEn.name: Global motion integration overriding the veridical local trajectories

impl.notes: Trails toggle showing the true straight paths.

first.where: Phenomenal characteristics of the peripheral drift illusion. Vision (Japan) 15: 261–262

entries.effectEn: A static image of concentric rings of coloured segments rotates steadily. Nothing moves; a screenshot rotates just as well.

mechanismEn.name: Asymmetric luminance-gradient sequences produce spurious motion signals; microsaccades and blinks trigger the jumps

entries.notesEn: Kitaoka image is under his copyright and is widely reposted without permission. Our version must be built from the published luminance rule, not traced.

impl.notes: Generate the rings procedurally rather than copying Kitaoka image — that is both the honest approach and the more interesting one, because the luminance sequence becomes a control. A slider over the four-step sequence lets the visitor destroy and rebuild the effect. Add a static-fixation test: stare at one point and it stops.

first.where: Rubber hands feel touch that eyes see. Nature 391(6669): 756

entries.effectEn: Watch a rubber hand being stroked while your own hidden hand is stroked in time, and within a minute the rubber hand feels like yours. Threaten it and you flinch.

mechanismEn.name: Vision, touch and proprioception are reconciled by reassigning body ownership — the cheapest way to make the three agree is to adopt the hand you can see

entries.notesEn: The demonstration that body ownership is inferred, not given. It reshaped how philosophers write about the self.

impl.notes: Cannot be done in a browser and we should not pretend. Ship a clear do-it-yourself protocol — rubber hand or a stuffed glove, a screen, two brushes, a helper, synchronous versus asynchronous stroking as the control — plus a filmed demonstration we shoot ourselves. The asynchronous condition is essential: without it this is a party trick rather than an experiment.

first.where: Synsoplevede Figurer. Doctoral thesis, Gyldendalske Boghandel, Copenhagen, 1915

entries.effectEn: A shape read either as a white vase on black, or as two black faces in profile on white — never both at once.

mechanismEn.name: Figure-ground assignment: whichever region owns the contour becomes the object, and the other becomes shapeless background

entries.notesEn: The key insight is not the flipping but the asymmetry: the background is not merely unattended, it has no shape at all.

impl.notes: Draw our own profile silhouette rather than using Rubin figure, and add contour-ownership cues the visitor can dial up to bias one reading. Generating the vase as a solid of revolution from a face profile is a nice touch and makes the relationship explicit.

first.where: Noted 1898; published as Dodge, Visual perception during eye movement. Psychological Review 7(5): 454–465, 1900

entries.effectEn: Vision is suppressed during each saccade, several times a second, and the gap is never noticed.

mechanismEn.name: Active suppression of the magnocellular pathway around saccade onset, plus masking by the pre- and post-saccadic images

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from visual/attention into the new eye-movement category. Binda and Morrone treat perisaccadic effects as one class of transient distortions of space, time and number; filing this under attention hid that.

impl.notes: The mirror demonstration needs no code at all: look at one eye in a mirror, then the other, and you will never catch the movement. Instructions plus a second person, plus the chronostasis stopped-clock demo, is the right exhibit. Honest about needing no screen.

first.where: The Peep-Show, London Hippodrome, 1921, in a scene called The Valley of Echoes

entries.effectEn: Changing the colour of stage light makes painted colours on a set or a costume vanish, darken to black, or change identity — a striped coat becomes plain, a made-up face changes complexion.

mechanismEn.name: A coloured surface reflects nothing under illumination lacking its wavelengths; the perceptual surprise is how completely the object disappears

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. The only entry in the catalogue whose first appearance is a variety show. Reaching it required searching the theatre-lighting trade literature rather than the perception literature — a reminder that the aggregators only index one of those.

impl.notes: A painted scene rendered under a controllable illuminant spectrum; dragging the illuminant makes objects disappear. Needs real spectral data to be honest rather than a naive RGB multiply.

first.by: Matthew Luckiesh (first printing); Friedrich Sander (1926, the name)
first.where: Luckiesh, Visual Illusions, 1922; Sander, Optische Täuschungen und Psychologie, Neue Psychologische Studien 1: 159–166, 1926

entries.effectEn: The two diagonals drawn inside a wide parallelogram look very different in length. They are equal.

mechanismEn.name: The diagonals are judged relative to the parallelograms they sit in rather than against each other

impl.notes: Slider on the shear angle; a button rotates one diagonal onto the other to prove equality.

first.where: Two-channel listening to musical scales. JASA 57(5): 1156–1160

entries.effectEn: An ascending and a descending scale are interleaved between the ears note by note. Listeners hear two smooth melodies, one high and one low, each coming cleanly from one ear — a reorganisation that discards the actual channel assignment entirely.

mechanismEn.name: Auditory scene analysis groups by pitch proximity and then assigns a location to each group, rather than grouping by location first

entries.notesEn: Composers have used the underlying trick for centuries — Tchaikovsky splits a melody between two instrument groups in the Sixth Symphony so that neither plays the tune the audience hears.

impl.notes: Headphones mandatory. The essential control is a per-channel solo: play the left channel alone and the listener hears the jagged sequence that is physically there, which contradicts what they just heard with both ears. Nothing else makes the point as well.

first.where: Ueber eine optische Inversion bei Betrachtung verkehrter physischer Bilder. Annalen der Physik 181(10): 298–311

entries.effectEn: A staircase seen from above, or the same staircase upside down seen from below.

mechanismEn.name: Perspective reversal: the drawing is consistent with two opposite surface orientations

impl.notes: Sugihara 3D Schröder Staircase (first prize, BIOTY 2020) is the version worth aiming at: a physical object that changes reading when a mirror or a rotation is introduced. Build the real geometry and let the camera do the work.

first.by: Elke Lingelbach; published by Schrauf, Lingelbach and Wist (1997)
first.where: The scintillating grid illusion. Vision Research 37(8): 1033–1038

entries.effectEn: Black dots flash on and off in the white discs at the intersections of a grey grid, always in peripheral vision.

mechanismEn.name: Related to but distinct from the Hermann grid; depends on the discs, on eye movements and on contrast in a way the Hermann grid does not

entries.notesEn: Discovered by accident in a private house, not in a laboratory — worth telling, because it is a reminder that this field is still open to amateurs.

impl.notes: Sliders on disc size, bar luminance and grid spacing. Adding a fixation cross makes the peripheral dependence obvious: the dot under the cross never scintillates.

first.by: Michael W. Karlovich and Pascal Wallisch
first.where: Scintillating starbursts: concentric star polygons induce illusory ray patterns. i-Perception 12(3)

entries.effectEn: Concentric star polygons produce bright rays radiating from the centre. There are no rays.

mechanismEn.name: Illusory contours completed across the polygon vertices, strengthened in peripheral vision and modulated by contrast and vertex count

entries.notesEn: Open access with a full parameter study, which makes an unusually faithful implementation possible.

impl.notes: Pure geometry, fully specified in an open-access paper: sliders on ring count, vertex count, contrast and line width reproduce the parameter study from the paper. One of the best build-to-research-quality candidates in the catalogue.

first.by: David C. Knill and Daniel Kersten
first.where: Apparent surface curvature affects lightness perception. Nature 351(6323): 228–230

entries.effectEn: Two shapes with identical luminance ramps look uniformly shaded when read as cylinders and sharply different when read as flat cubes. The pixels are the same.

mechanismEn.name: Perceived 3D shape determines how a luminance gradient is split between illumination and reflectance

impl.notes: Two ramp pairs with a toggle switching the bounding contours between curved and straight. The pixels never change; only the outline does. Pairs with checker-shadow as the two-sentence version of the whole lightness argument.

first.where: Perception of shape from shading. Nature 331(6152): 163–166

entries.effectEn: Discs shaded light-at-top read as bumps, discs shaded light-at-bottom read as dents. Turn the page and they swap.

mechanismEn.name: The visual system assumes a single light source above, which is a good bet on a planet with one sun

entries.notesEn: Also the crater illusion, which is the same prior applied to satellite photographs.

impl.notes: Grid of shaded discs with a light-direction dial. Rotating the light past horizontal flips the whole grid at once, which is a striking moment and costs almost nothing to build.

first.where: Mind Sights, W. H. Freeman, 1990, p. 79

entries.effectEn: An elephant whose legs cannot be counted: the gaps between the legs are also legs, and every attempt to resolve it fails.

mechanismEn.name: Figure-ground ambiguity exploited locally: the spaces are given feet, so the visual system cannot settle which regions own the contours

entries.notesEn: The same Shepard as the tabletop illusion and the Shepard tone. Three entries in this catalogue from one person, in three different modalities.

impl.notes: Draw our own animal rather than copying Shepard. A slider that slides the feet back to the correct verticals resolves it, which is a better explanation than any caption.

first.where: Psychophysical complementarity, in Perceptual Organization (Kubovy and Pomerantz, eds.), Lawrence Erlbaum, 1981, pp. 297–299; the strong version in Mind Sights, W. H. Freeman, 1990

entries.effectEn: Two tabletops drawn as identical parallelograms in different orientations look wildly different in proportion. Rotating one onto the other shows they coincide exactly.

mechanismEn.name: Automatic interpretation of the parallelogram as a rectangle in depth, with foreshortening undone along the apparent depth axis

entries.notesEn: Among the strongest illusions known — it does not weaken when you know the answer. Date corrected in W13 after an adversarial audit.

impl.notes: The demo is the animation: one tabletop lifts off, rotates and lands on the other. Add a stripped mode that removes the legs, where the effect weakens but survives.

first.where: Circularity in judgments of relative pitch. JASA 36(12): 2346–2353

entries.effectEn: A scale that rises forever without ever getting higher.

mechanismEn.name: Octave-spaced sine components under a fixed bell-shaped spectral envelope: pitch chroma moves while pitch height stays put, so the two cues are decoupled

entries.notesEn: Used deliberately in the Batman and Dunkirk soundtracks and in the Super Mario 64 endless staircase. Worth noting on the page: people have heard this illusion far more often than they know.

impl.notes: Web Audio: a bank of oscillators at octave spacing under a Gaussian gain envelope in log frequency, with sliders on envelope width, step size and rate. A spectrum view alongside makes the mechanism visible instead of magical. Requires a user gesture to start audio — every browser blocks autoplay.

first.by: Jordan W. Suchow and George A. Alvarez
first.where: Motion silences awareness of visual change. Current Biology 21(2): 140–143
