entries.effectEn: A ring of dots changing colour rapidly appears to stop changing the moment the ring starts to rotate. The changes continue at exactly the same rate.

mechanismEn.name: Global motion plus crowding: the change signal is swamped once the objects move
mechanismEn.by: Suchow and Alvarez 2011; Turi and Burr 2013 on crowding

entries.notesEn: Among the most startling entries in the catalogue, and among the cheapest to build — a rare combination.

impl.notes: Ring of dots, rotation-speed slider, and a change-type selector (hue, luminance, size, shape). Freezing rotation while the changes continue is the whole demonstration and must be a single button.

first.where: De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs. Pitois-Levrault, Paris, 1839

entries.effectEn: A grey patch looks lighter on a dark surround and darker on a light one, although the patch never changes.

mechanismEn.name: Lateral inhibition at an early stage
Inference about illumination and surface, a higher-level process
mechanismEn.by: Helmholtz tradition; see Kingdom 1997 on the two legacies

entries.notesEn: Chevreul was hired to fix a dyeing complaint at the Gobelins works and ended up writing the book that the Impressionists read.

impl.notes: The canonical two-square demo, plus a drag that slides one patch out of its surround and into the other — the moment of arrival is the whole point.

first.by: William S. Cleveland and Robert McGill (earliest description); named by Ross H. Day and Erica J. Stecher (1991)
first.where: Cleveland and McGill, JASA 79(387): 531–554, 1984; Day and Stecher, Sine of an illusion. Perception 20(1): 49–55, 1991

entries.effectEn: Vertical bars of identical length arranged along a sine curve appear to shrink where the curve is steep.

mechanismEn.name: The visual system judges the extent perpendicular to the local curve direction rather than the true vertical extent

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. Day and Stecher argue it is the Müller-Lyer illusion in another costume. Directly relevant to charting: it is why error bands and candlestick plots mislead.

impl.notes: Bars along a curve with an amplitude slider and a toggle that straightens the curve. Directly relevant to charting, which makes it a good bridge to a data-visualisation audience.

first.by: Robert E. Remez, Philip E. Rubin, David B. Pisoni and Thomas D. Carrell
first.where: Speech perception without traditional speech cues. Science 212(4497): 947–949

entries.effectEn: Three whistling tones tracking the formants of a sentence sound like electronic noise — until you are told what the sentence is, after which you cannot hear anything else.

mechanismEn.name: Speech perception depends on time-varying patterns rather than on the acoustic detail of natural speech; once the speech mode engages, it does not disengage

entries.notesEn: Like Mooney faces, this cannot be experienced twice. Design the page accordingly.

impl.notes: Requires formant tracking on our own recordings, which is real work — but the payoff is the best one-way-door demonstration in the catalogue alongside Mooney faces. Strict order of presentation: noise first, then the sentence, then the noise again. The page must not spoil it above the fold.

first.by: Alfred H. Holway and Edwin G. Boring (the definitive experiment); described far earlier by Descartes and Berkeley
first.where: Determinants of apparent visual size with distance variant. The American Journal of Psychology 54(1): 21–37

entries.effectEn: An object keeps its apparent size as it recedes, even though its retinal image shrinks in proportion to distance. Remove the depth cues and the constancy collapses.

mechanismEn.name: Perceived size is retinal size scaled by perceived distance — which is why so many size illusions are really distance illusions

entries.notesEn: Catalogued as a capacity, like colour constancy. The Ponzo, Ames room, Shepard tables and moon illusions are all this mechanism being exploited.

impl.notes: A corridor scene with a toggle that strips depth cues one at a time (texture gradient, linear perspective, occlusion, shadow) while an object recedes. Watching apparent size come unglued as the cues go is the explanatory core of the whole depth section.

first.where: Analyse expérimentale de quelques éléments de la sensation de poids. Archives de Physiologie Normale et Pathologique 3: 122–135

entries.effectEn: Two boxes of identical weight and different size. The smaller one feels substantially heavier, and keeps feeling heavier however many times you check.

mechanismEn.name: Expected weight is subtracted from felt weight; the expectation is wrong and the error is what you feel. The illusion persists after the expectation is corrected, which is why it is still argued about

entries.notesEn: The important part is that knowing does not help. It is a straightforward counterexample to the idea that illusions are errors that understanding can correct.

impl.notes: Do-it-yourself: two different-sized containers loaded to the same mass with a kitchen scale, and a photograph of the scale readings. Trivially reproducible at home and completely convincing, which is a rare combination.

first.where: Observationes et curationes medicae, Utrecht, 1664

entries.effectEn: Waking unable to move, with a crushing weight on the chest and the certain presence of an intruder in the room. The paralysis is real; the intruder is not.

mechanismEn.name: REM atonia persisting into waking, with dream imagery overlaid on the real bedroom, and a threat-vigilance system running with no way to act

entries.notesEn: Probably the most widely experienced illusion in the entire catalogue: lifetime prevalence estimates run from 8 to 40 per cent, and almost none of the standard illusion indexes list it.

impl.notes: Explanation only, with the cross-cultural names — the Old Hag, kanashibari, домовой давит — which are the same experience given a local explanation. That comparison is the most interesting thing a page can do with it.

first.where: Lightness perception and lightness illusions, in The New Cognitive Neurosciences, 2nd ed. MIT Press, pp. 339–351

entries.effectEn: Identical grey diamonds look different against a snaking striped ground, and the effect survives removal of the cues that were supposed to explain it.

mechanismEn.name: Contested — the anti-snake control version removes the apparent illumination cue and much of the effect remains

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. The anti-snake control is the argument: removing the apparent illumination cue leaves much of the effect standing, which is a problem for the accounts that invoke it.

impl.notes: Snake and anti-snake versions side by side with a switch, which is how the argument is actually made.

first.by: Ashton Graybiel (the oculogravic illusion, its visual counterpart)
first.where: Graybiel, The oculogravic illusion. AMA Archives of Ophthalmology 48(5): 605–615, 1952

entries.effectEn: Acceleration on take-off feels exactly like pitching up, because the otoliths cannot tell the two apart. Pilots push the nose down into the sea.

mechanismEn.name: Otolith organs measure the sum of gravity and linear acceleration and cannot decompose it — a genuine physical ambiguity, not a processing failure

entries.notesEn: The best example in the catalogue of an illusion that is not a defect at all: the sensor is reporting exactly what it measures, and the information needed to disambiguate is not physically present.

impl.notes: A vector diagram the visitor can drag: gravity plus acceleration, with the resultant labelled as what the otoliths report. The ambiguity becomes obvious in one interaction.

first.where: The role of auditory cues in modulating the perceived crispness and staleness of potato chips. Journal of Sensory Studies 19(5): 347–363

entries.effectEn: Amplify the crunch a person hears as they bite, especially above 2 kHz, and the crisp tastes fresher and crisper. The crisp has not changed.

mechanismEn.name: Food texture is judged from sound as well as from the mouth; the auditory channel is weighted more heavily than anyone expected

entries.notesEn: Shares its pipeline with the parchment-skin illusion — one audio-feedback component serves both.

impl.notes: Genuinely buildable in a browser: microphone capture, a high-shelf filter, headphone feedback, and a bag of crisps the visitor supplies. Needs microphone permission, low latency and a clear opt-in. Almost nobody has done this on the web and it would be the most memorable page on the site.

first.by: Anne-Sylvie Crisinel, Charles Spence and colleagues
first.where: A bittersweet symphony. Food Quality and Preference 24(1): 201–204

entries.effectEn: The same toffee tastes about ten per cent more bitter with low-pitched music and ten per cent sweeter with high-pitched music.

mechanismEn.name: Consistent crossmodal correspondences between pitch, timbre and basic tastes, which shift the criterion applied to an ambiguous flavour

entries.notesEn: Commercially deployed by airlines and chocolate makers, which makes it one of the few illusions in the catalogue with a revenue model.

impl.notes: Two soundtracks, one piece of chocolate the visitor supplies, and a rating scale. Low effort, real result, and it sends people away from the screen with something to do.

first.by: Ladan Shams, Yukiyasu Kamitani and Shinsuke Shimojo
first.where: What you see is what you hear. Nature 408(6814): 788

entries.effectEn: One flash accompanied by two beeps is seen as two flashes.

mechanismEn.name: Sound wins where it is the more reliable sense: audition has far better temporal resolution than vision, so it dominates the count

entries.notesEn: Notable for going the unusual direction — almost every other crossmodal illusion has vision overriding hearing.

impl.notes: One of the few crossmodal illusions that works properly in a browser. Needs precise audio-visual synchronisation: schedule the beeps on the AudioContext clock and the flashes on requestAnimationFrame, and measure the offset rather than assuming it. Sliders on beep count and interval; peripheral presentation strengthens it.

first.where: Discovered while editing spoken commentary for the CD Musical Illusions and Paradoxes (1995); published as Deutsch, Henthorn and Lapidis, Illusory transformation from speech to song. JASA 129(4): 2245–2252, 2011

entries.effectEn: An ordinary spoken phrase repeated exactly, without any change at all, stops sounding like speech and starts sounding like singing. It cannot be undone.

mechanismEn.name: Repetition shifts processing from a speech mode to a music mode; pitch contours that were incidental become a melody

entries.notesEn: The best entry point in the catalogue to the question of where speech ends and music begins. Also irreversible: once a phrase sings, it sings forever.

impl.notes: Record our own phrases — in Russian, Belarusian and English — and loop them with a repetition counter. Whether the effect works equally across the three languages is an open and genuinely interesting question, and asking visitors to report when it flips would produce real data.

first.where: Flash animation published by Procreo Flash Design Laboratory, 2003

entries.effectEn: A silhouetted dancer spins clockwise or anticlockwise, and switches. Both readings fit the image exactly.

mechanismEn.name: A silhouette carries no occlusion or shading cue to depth order, so the structure-from-motion solution is genuinely ambiguous

entries.notesEn: The widespread claim that the spin direction reveals left- or right-brain dominance is false and was invented by a newspaper in 2007. The page should say so directly — this is the most-repeated piece of misinformation attached to any illusion in the catalogue.

impl.notes: Render our own silhouette from a rotating 3D figure, with a shading slider that restores depth cues and locks the direction. The disambiguation control is what turns a viral image into an explanation.

first.where: Footsteps and inchworms: illusions show that contrast affects apparent speed. Perception 30(7): 785–794; extended in Vision Research 44(18): 2171–2178 (2004)

entries.effectEn: Two rectangles slide across a striped background at a constant, identical speed, and appear to take alternating steps like feet.

mechanismEn.name: Apparent speed depends on contrast: when a rectangle edge matches the stripe it crosses, its contrast drops and it appears to slow or stop

impl.notes: Canvas animation with sliders on rectangle luminance and stripe contrast. Setting both rectangles to mid-grey removes the stepping entirely — the control that makes the explanation land.

first.by: Wolfgang Metzger (the ambiguous display); Sekuler, Sekuler and Lau (1997) added the sound
first.where: Metzger, Beobachtungen über phänomenale Identität. Psychologische Forschung 19: 1–60; Sekuler et al., Sound alters visual motion perception. Nature 385(6614): 308

entries.effectEn: Two identical discs crossing each other are ambiguous — they stream through or bounce off. A single click at the moment of coincidence makes them bounce, decisively.

mechanismEn.name: The sound supplies evidence for a collision, and the ambiguous visual motion is resolved in favour of the interpretation that a collision implies

entries.notesEn: One of the cheapest convincing crossmodal demonstrations available, and it works on laptop speakers.

impl.notes: Easy and very effective: two discs, a click toggle, and a slider on when the click occurs relative to coincidence. The effect has a narrow timing window that visitors can find themselves.

first.where: Die stroboscopischen Scheiben, oder optischen Zauberscheiben. Trentsensky und Vieweg, 1833

entries.effectEn: Under intermittent light, cyclic motion appears frozen, slowed or reversed.

mechanismEn.name: Sampling below the Nyquist rate for the motion frequency

entries.notesEn: The apparatus that made cinema possible, invented to study perception.

impl.notes: Shares the renderer with wagon-wheel; the exhibit is the history, including the phenakistiscope discs.

first.by: John Ridley Stroop; published in German by Jaensch in 1929
first.where: Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology 18(6): 643–662

entries.effectEn: Naming the ink colour of a colour word is much slower when the word says a different colour. Reading is automatic and cannot be switched off.

mechanismEn.name: Word reading is more automatic than colour naming, so the irrelevant dimension intrudes and has to be suppressed

entries.notesEn: A cognitive rather than a perceptual illusion, but too useful and too well suited to a web page to leave out.

impl.notes: Timed congruent and incongruent blocks with a keyboard response; report the visitor own interference cost in milliseconds. Genuinely interesting in three languages — a Russian-Belarusian bilingual doing the task in both should show something, and the site is uniquely placed to ask.

first.where: Ambiguous cylinders: a new class of impossible objects. Computer Aided Drafting, Design and Manufacturing 25(3): 19–25

entries.effectEn: A row of objects that are circles in direct view and squares in a mirror behind them. Rotating them 180 degrees swaps which is which.

mechanismEn.name: One curved silhouette can project to two different outlines from two viewpoints; the visual system assumes the simplest solid consistent with each view independently

entries.notesEn: Sugihara construction is fully specified in the paper, so we can implement the mathematics rather than copy a model.

impl.notes: Compute the cylinder wall from two target silhouettes — the construction is in the paper — and render with a virtual mirror. Also export STL so visitors can print one. The 3D-printable export is a strong reason to build it properly.

first.by: Recorded since antiquity; Hevelius drew the 1661 Danzig display
first.where: Minnaert 1954; Hevelius, Mercurius in Sole visus, 1662

entries.effectEn: Two bright patches flanking the sun at the same height, often with a coloured tail. Frequently reported as a second and third sun.

mechanismEn.name: Refraction through horizontally oriented plate-shaped ice crystals, which fixes the patches at the sun elevation

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: Adaptation, after-effect and contrast in the perception of curved lines. Journal of Experimental Psychology 16(1): 1–31

entries.effectEn: Run a finger along a curved edge for a minute and a straight edge afterwards feels curved the other way.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation of curvature-tuned mechanisms, exactly parallel to the visual tilt aftereffect

entries.notesEn: Refiled in W18 from tactile/touch-location. It is a curvature aftereffect — a shape phenomenon — and Hayward gives tactile aftereffects their own class.

impl.notes: A printable pair of 3D-printable or cardboard edges — one curved, one straight — plus timing instructions. Cheap and it works.

first.by: Georg Andreas Sorge; Giuseppe Tartini reported hearing it in 1714 and published in 1754
first.where: Sorge, Vorgemach der musicalischen Composition, 1745; Tartini, Trattato di musica, 1754

entries.effectEn: Two loud pure tones produce a third, lower tone that is not in the air at all.

mechanismEn.name: Nonlinear distortion in the cochlea generates energy at the difference frequency

entries.notesEn: Violinists still use it: play a double stop in tune and the third tone appears, which makes it an intonation check.

impl.notes: Two oscillators with independent frequency sliders and a readout of the predicted difference tone. Needs reasonable volume to work, so the page must warn about level before it starts.

first.where: The tau effect: an example of psychological relativity. Science 71(1847): 536–537

entries.effectEn: Three taps equally spaced along the arm feel unequally spaced if the intervals between them are unequal. Time distorts felt distance.

mechanismEn.name: A Bayesian prior for constant speed: if the timing says one gap was shorter, the distance must have been shorter too

entries.notesEn: The mirror image of the kappa effect: there space distorts time, here time distorts space.

impl.notes: Same rig as the cutaneous rabbit — the two illusions are the same prior seen from different angles and should share one exhibit.

first.where: Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt III: Experimentelle Untersuchungen über phänomenale Identität. Psychologische Forschung 7: 81–136

entries.effectEn: Three dots shifting one position are seen either as the whole group jumping together, or as one end dot leaping over the others — and which one you see depends only on the blank interval between frames.

mechanismEn.name: Two motion systems with different time constants competing to solve the correspondence problem

impl.notes: Three dots with an interstimulus-interval slider in milliseconds. The switch from element motion to group motion happens around 50 ms and the visitor can find their own crossover — a real individual measurement.

first.where: Margaret Thatcher: a new illusion. Perception 9(4): 483–484

entries.effectEn: A face with the eyes and mouth flipped upside down looks almost normal while the whole face is inverted, and grotesque the moment it is turned upright.

mechanismEn.name: Configural face processing works only on upright faces; inverted, the face is processed feature by feature and the local flips go unnoticed

entries.notesEn: Do not use Thatcher. Using a public figure is both a rights problem and unnecessary; the effect works on any face.

impl.notes: Needs a face we have rights to. Use our own photographs, with a continuous rotation slider rather than a two-state flip — the point at which grotesqueness appears is around 90 to 120 degrees and finding it is the interesting part.

first.by: John Ayrton Paris (usually credited); possibly Peter Mark Roget or William Henry Fitton
first.where: Paris, Philosophy in Sport Made Science in Earnest, 1827

entries.effectEn: A disc with a bird on one side and a cage on the other, spun on strings, shows the bird in the cage.

mechanismEn.name: Traditionally explained by persistence of vision; the modern account is temporal integration by the visual system, which is not the same thing
mechanismEn.by: Anderson and Anderson 1978 on the myth

entries.notesEn: Catalogued as apparatus rather than illusion proper, but it belongs: it is where the public first met the idea that vision could be tricked systematically.

impl.notes: A WebGL disc the visitor spins by dragging, with a speed readout and the two faces separable. Good opening exhibit for a history section on pre-cinema optical toys.

first.by: Cecilia Bleasdale (photograph); Caitlin McNeill (posted it to Tumblr, 26 February 2015)
first.where: Tumblr and then the entire internet; scientific analysis in Lafer-Sousa, Hermann and Conway, Current Biology 25(13): R545–R546

entries.effectEn: One photograph of one dress is seen as blue and black by some observers and white and gold by others, stably, with no way to switch.

mechanismEn.name: Ambiguous illumination: observers who assume a bluish daylight discount blue and see white and gold; those who assume warm artificial light see blue and black
Correlates with chronotype — early risers, exposed to more daylight, more often see white and gold

entries.notesEn: The single most important modern illusion for the general public, because it made individual differences in perception undeniable. Also the point at which vision science acquired a mass audience.

impl.notes: We cannot republish the copyrighted photograph. Build the mechanism instead: our own rendered fabric under a slider that moves the illuminant from tungsten to overcast daylight, with the pixel values held constant. That teaches what the photograph only demonstrates.

first.where: Uppsala Läkareförenings Förhandlingar 2: 489–495, 1896

entries.effectEn: A grid of interleaved warm bars at 40 °C and cool bars at 20 °C. Touch it and it burns — although neither temperature is anywhere near painful alone.

mechanismEn.name: Cool-sensitive pathways normally inhibit a pain pathway; the warm bars remove that inhibition and pain is reported from harmless stimuli

entries.notesEn: Included for completeness and deliberately not turned into a demonstration. The catalogue documents it; the site does not invite anyone to try it.

impl.notes: Buildable with alternating copper tubes and two water baths, but it produces genuine pain and the temperature margin for safety is not wide. Explanation and video only. Do not publish a build guide.

first.where: Localization of thermal sensation: an illusion and synthetic heat. Perception & Psychophysics 22(4): 331–337

entries.effectEn: Three fingers on a surface, only the outer two warmed, and all three feel warm. Temperature is referred to skin nothing is heating.

mechanismEn.name: Thermal localisation is poor and is resolved using the tactile map: where you feel touch is where you feel temperature

entries.notesEn: The safe member of the thermal family. The thermal grill next to it is documented and deliberately not buildable.

impl.notes: Do-it-yourself with three coins, two warmed. Simple, safe, and unlike the thermal grill it can be published as a build.

first.by: James J. Gibson and Minnie Radner
first.where: Adaptation, after-effect and contrast in the perception of tilted lines. Journal of Experimental Psychology 20(5): 453–467

entries.effectEn: Stare at a tilted grating for a minute and a vertical one afterwards appears tilted the other way.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation of orientation-tuned cells shifts the population response away from the adapted orientation

entries.notesEn: The temporal twin of the tilt illusion; both from the same pair of 1937 papers.

impl.notes: Timed adaptation then a nulling task — the visitor rotates a test grating to vertical and the page records the error in degrees. Shares machinery with the tilt illusion exhibit.

first.by: James J. Gibson and Minnie Radner
first.where: Adaptation, after-effect and contrast in the perception of tilted lines. I. Quantitative studies. Journal of Experimental Psychology 20(5): 453–467

entries.effectEn: A grating looks tilted away from its true orientation when surrounded by a grating at a different angle.

mechanismEn.name: Lateral inhibition between orientation-tuned cells in V1, repulsive at small angle differences and attractive at large ones

entries.notesEn: Twinned with the tilt aftereffect, catalogued separately under adaptation.

impl.notes: Centre and surround gratings on canvas, slider on surround angle; plotting the visitor matching error against surround angle reproduces the classic repulsion-then-attraction curve.

first.where: Minnaert 1954; Lynch and Livingston 2001

entries.effectEn: Distant objects stretched vertically into towers, or squashed flat, by the air between.

mechanismEn.name: Differential refraction through a temperature-stratified atmosphere, magnifying or compressing the vertical dimension only

entries.notesEn: Physical optics: the image is in the light, and a camera is fooled too. Catalogued to mark the boundary that makes the perceptual entries meaningful.

first.where: A musical paradox. Music Perception 3(3): 275–280

entries.effectEn: Two tones a tritone apart. Some listeners hear the pair rising, others hear the identical pair falling, and each is completely certain.

mechanismEn.name: Each listener has an orientation of the pitch-class circle fixed relative to their own speech range; tones in the upper half of that circle are heard as higher
The orientation tracks the language and dialect the listener grew up with — Californians and southern English listeners give opposite answers

entries.notesEn: The strongest evidence in the catalogue that perception is shaped by the language you learned as a child. For a trilingual site this is the most interesting entry of all.

impl.notes: The full pitch-class battery: twelve pairs, forced choice up or down, then plot the visitor own circle. With visitors in three language communities the site can collect something genuinely interesting — but that means asking about language background, and asking properly, with consent and no personal data.

first.where: Über das Verschwinden gegebener Gegenstände innerhalb unseres Gesichtskreises. Ophthalmologische Bibliothek 2(2): 1–53

entries.effectEn: Hold your gaze on one point and unchanging things elsewhere in the field simply stop being there.

mechanismEn.name: Neural adaptation to unchanging input; fixational eye movements normally prevent it, and the illusion is what happens when they are insufficient

entries.notesEn: The demonstration that vision is built for change and goes blind to constancy. Also the mechanism behind the lilac chaser.

impl.notes: Fixation dot plus a soft-edged coloured blob in the periphery, with a timer showing how long the visitor held fixation before it vanished. Blur is essential — hard edges resist fading.

first.by: Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī (the geometric device); as an illusion, Shapiro and Rose-Henig (2013)
first.where: al-Ṭūsī, Taḥrīr al-Majisṭī, 1247; Tusi or not Tusi, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2013 (second prize)

entries.effectEn: A point on a small circle rolling inside a circle of twice the diameter traces a straight line — and the eye refuses to see it as straight.

mechanismEn.name: Rotational motion signals dominate over the veridical linear trajectory of any single point

entries.notesEn: Also a nice piece of history: the device was invented to fix a problem in Ptolemaic astronomy.

impl.notes: Pure geometry, trivially exact, with a trail toggle proving the path is a diameter. One of the cheapest convincing builds available.

first.where: Two-Stroke Apparent Motion, Best Illusion of the Year Contest 2005 (second prize)

entries.effectEn: Two frames alternated with a contrast reversal produce continuous motion in one direction forever, from a two-frame loop.

mechanismEn.name: Combines ordinary apparent motion with reverse phi so that the return stroke is seen as continuing rather than reversing

impl.notes: Pairs with reverse-phi in one exhibit; the shared control is the contrast inversion toggle.

first.by: Gustav Kuhn and Michael F. Land
first.where: There is more to magic than meets the eye. Current Biology 16(22): R950–R951

entries.effectEn: A magician throws a ball up twice, then mimes a third throw while palming it. Sixty-three per cent of observers see the ball rise and vanish in mid-air.

mechanismEn.name: Social cues drive the illusion: observers who saw the phantom ball had followed the magician eyes upward, not his hand. Expectation plus gaze cueing constructs an event that did not occur

entries.notesEn: Opens the whole class of illusions that were working professional techniques for centuries before anyone studied them. Stage magic is a research literature the perception indexes do not cite.

impl.notes: Film our own version, with three cuts: normal, the magician face occluded, and the magician looking at his hand. The effect drops with each. That comparison is a whole psychology lecture in ninety seconds.

first.where: Grundlinien der Lehre von den Bewegungsempfindungen. Engelmann, Leipzig, 1875

entries.effectEn: Sitting in a stationary train while the train on the next platform pulls out, and feeling yourself move.

mechanismEn.name: Large-field visual motion is normally caused by self-motion, so the visual system reports self-motion; the vestibular system disagrees and loses

entries.notesEn: The reason VR makes people sick: vection without matching vestibular input is exactly the conflict that produces nausea.

impl.notes: Works in a browser if the display fills enough of the visual field: a full-screen textured tunnel or a rotating striped drum, best on a phone held close. Warn about motion sickness before it starts and provide an immediate stop. This is the entry that most needs a comfort warning.

first.by: Ian P. Howard and William B. Templeton (named and analysed)
first.where: Human Spatial Orientation. Wiley, 1966

entries.effectEn: Sound is heard as coming from wherever a plausible visual source is — the puppet, the screen, the loudspeaker you can see rather than the one you cannot.

mechanismEn.name: Vision has better spatial resolution than hearing, so the brain weights it more heavily and the auditory estimate is pulled toward it

entries.notesEn: The reason cinema sound works at all: the dialogue comes from speakers beside the screen and is heard from the actor mouth.

impl.notes: Headphones plus an on-screen mouth animation whose horizontal position the visitor can drag independently of the audio panning. Watching the perceived source follow the picture rather than the pan is the demonstration.

first.where: De errore quodam optico asymmetria bulbi oculi effecto. Dissertation, Koch, Marburg, 1851

entries.effectEn: A vertical line looks longer than a horizontal line of the same length; the effect is strongest in an inverted T, where bisection adds to it.

mechanismEn.name: Two effects added together: an anisotropy favouring the vertical, plus a bisection effect that shortens the divided line

entries.notesEn: Explains the Gateway Arch in St Louis, which is as wide as it is tall and looks much taller.

impl.notes: Three panels side by side: L, T and inverted T, each with a drag handle. Separating the anisotropy from the bisection component is the point of the demo.

first.by: James T. Walker, Reta C. Rupich and Jack L. Powell
first.where: The vista paradox: a natural visual illusion. Perception & Psychophysics 46(6): 599–608

entries.effectEn: A distant object seen through a window appears to shrink as you walk toward the window.

mechanismEn.name: The distant object is assigned the distance of the aperture; as the aperture gets nearer, the object perceived distance shrinks with it and so does its perceived size

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9.

impl.notes: WebGL room with a window and a distant mountain, and a dolly control. The rendered visual angle can be plotted against perceived size to show they diverge.

first.by: Ottomar Rosenbach; named moving visual phantoms by Tynan and Sekuler (1975)
first.where: Rosenbach, Zeitschrift für Psychologie 29: 434–448, 1902; Tynan and Sekuler, Science 188(4191): 951–952, 1975

entries.effectEn: A moving grating interrupted by a blank strip is completed across the strip: a faint ghost grating is seen drifting through empty space.

mechanismEn.name: Surface completion across an occluder, gated by brightness and contrast rather than by motion as such

entries.notesEn: Resolved in W9. Another case where the effect waited seventy years for a name.

impl.notes: Animated grating with an adjustable blank strip; the phantom needs low spatial frequency and slow drift to appear.

first.by: Simon Stampfer and Joseph Plateau (stroboscopic discs); in film, from the earliest projection
first.where: Stampfer, Die stroboscopischen Scheiben, 1833

entries.effectEn: A spoked wheel filmed or strobed appears to turn slowly backwards, stand still, or crawl forwards.

mechanismEn.name: Temporal aliasing when the sampling rate beats against the spoke frequency
mechanismEn.by: straightforward under strobed or filmed light

mechanismEn.name: Discrete sampling by the visual system itself, to explain reports under continuous illumination

entries.notesEn: One of the few illusions in the catalogue where the interesting question is whether the illusion happens at all under some conditions.

impl.notes: Two panels: one animated at the display refresh rate (aliasing), one rendered with motion blur (no aliasing). Sliders on spoke count and rotation rate. The comparison is what makes the continuous-light controversy intelligible.

first.where: Un effetto di colorazione, in Il laboratorio e la città: XXI Congresso degli Psicologi Italiani. Società Italiana di Psicologia, Milano, 1987

entries.effectEn: A white area enclosed by a bright wavy line that is itself edged by a darker line takes on a faint wash of the bright line colour, spreading right across the enclosed area.

mechanismEn.name: Colour spreads from the inner boundary across the surface, and simultaneously the region becomes a figure rather than a hole

entries.notesEn: Unusually strong for a colour illusion: the tint is faint but it covers a large area and survives being looked at directly.

impl.notes: Procedural wavy contours in SVG with independent colour pickers for the two lines. Swapping the two colours reverses which region gets tinted — the cleanest way to show the effect belongs to the boundary pair, not to the enclosed shape.

first.where: A new effect of pattern on perceived lightness. Perception 8(4): 413–416

entries.effectEn: Identical grey patches embedded in the black and white stripes of a grating look different — and in the direction opposite to what simultaneous contrast predicts.

mechanismEn.name: Belongingness: the patch takes its lightness from the stripe it is seen as part of
Multiscale spatial filtering reproduces it without any grouping

entries.notesEn: The single most useful test case in lightness perception, precisely because it goes the wrong way for contrast accounts.

impl.notes: Grating with patch length as a slider. Long patches strengthen the effect, which is the observation the two competing theories argue about — worth stating on the page as an open question rather than an explained one.

first.by: Gil Morrot, Frédéric Brochet and Denis Dubourdieu
first.where: The color of odors. Brain and Language 79(2): 309–320

entries.effectEn: Oenology students given a white wine dyed red described it with red-wine vocabulary.

mechanismEn.name: Colour sets an expectation that reorganises how the smell is categorised and described

entries.notesEn: Routinely overstated in popular accounts as proof that experts cannot tell red from white. The study does not show that. Correcting the legend is more useful than repeating it.

impl.notes: Explanation only. If it is ever demonstrated live, the control — same wine, undyed, same tasters — is the part that matters, and the popular retellings always drop it.

first.where: Die geometrisch-optischen Täuschungen. Abhandlungen der Mathematisch-Physischen Klasse der Königlich-Sächsischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften 42: 55–178

entries.effectEn: Two straight vertical lines look bowed inward against a background of lines converging from outside them.

mechanismEn.name: Angle expansion at the intersections; the effect is largest for intersect angles of 10 to 30 degrees

entries.notesEn: Wundt 1898 monograph is also the closest thing the nineteenth century produced to this catalogue.

impl.notes: Share the renderer with the Hering illusion; one flag flips the fan geometry.

first.by: Katie Hetzel (found it), Roland Szabo (posted it); May 2018
first.where: A synthesised pronunciation of laurel from vocabulary.com, reposted to Instagram and Reddit

entries.effectEn: One recording. Roughly half of listeners hear Laurel and half hear Yanny, and neither group can produce the other reading at will.

mechanismEn.name: The clip carries acoustic evidence for both words in different frequency bands; which one you get depends on your hearing, your playback equipment and which band you weight
Shifting the spectral balance moves listeners from one percept to the other, which is what makes it demonstrable rather than mysterious

entries.notesEn: The auditory counterpart to the dress, three years later, and it did the same job: it made individual differences in perception undeniable to a mass audience.

impl.notes: The original recording is not ours to republish. Synthesise our own ambiguous token with the same spectral design and give visitors a tilt slider that moves the balance between the low and high bands — which turns a viral curiosity into an explanation. Age matters here too, since high-frequency hearing declines; worth asking.

first.where: On the properties of the Daedaleum, a new instrument of optical illusion. London and Edinburgh Philosophical Magazine 4: 36–41

entries.effectEn: A slitted drum of drawings spun on its axis shows continuous animation.

mechanismEn.name: Beta movement, with the slits providing the shutter that separates successive images

impl.notes: A WebGL drum seen from outside with the viewer positioned at a slit. Building it as real geometry rather than a flipbook is the point — the visitor should be able to slow it until the trick falls apart.

first.where: Ueber eine neue Art von Pseudoskopie. Annalen der Physik und Chemie 186(7): 500–525

entries.effectEn: Long parallel lines crossed by short oblique hatching look convergent or divergent.

mechanismEn.name: Orientation contrast between the hatch marks and the main lines, amplified by lateral inhibition between orientation-tuned cells

entries.notesEn: Historically the ancestor of the Poggendorff illusion — one figure, two named effects.

impl.notes: Sliders on hatch angle and hatch spacing; the effect peaks near 10–30 degrees and disappears at 0 and 90, which the visitor can find themselves.

first.where: Negative afterimage in hearing. JASA 36(12): 2413–2415

entries.effectEn: Listen to broadband noise with a narrow band removed, then switch it off, and a faint tone is heard at the frequency of the missing band.

mechanismEn.name: Adaptation in the surrounding frequency channels unbalances the population response, leaving the unadapted channel apparently active — the auditory analogue of a negative afterimage

entries.notesEn: A useful bridge for the site: an aftereffect that is unmistakably the same idea as a visual afterimage, in a different sense.

impl.notes: Notched noise via a biquad band-stop filter, a few seconds of exposure, then silence. Sliders on notch frequency and width. Works best on headphones at a moderate level; it is faint and needs a quiet room, which the page should say.
